entries.title: FBI Probes Hackers' Claim of Stealing Employee Data, Compromising Jobs Website
entries.summary: The FBI jobs portal remained offline after the group claimed to hack the site.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

The FBI said Wednesday that it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claims that it had stolen “very sensitive data” belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website.

“The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information," the FBI said in a statement. It said that while the “point of breach” was undetermined, "we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”

The jobs website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline as of Wednesday afternoon.

A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack.

“We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job,” said the ShinyHunters message, which was directed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Brett Leatherman, the assistant director in charge of the bureau's cyber division.

The claims could not immediately be verified. An email to an address associated with ShinyHunters was not immediately returned.

The hackers are seeking retribution over an FBI advisory

Miriam Wugmeister, a lawyer specializing in data, privacy and cybercrime who tracks hacking outfits like ShinyHunters, said that based on the group's past practices, there was reason to believe the hackers' claims, “so I think it’s likely that they were able to compromise this website and they got some data.”

She said that though the data that appeared to be compromised was the type of personal information that is routinely accessed during a breach, the hack nonetheless had alarming national security implications given that it could expose agents and their families to extortion, swatting and other harassment and because the identities of spouses were also said to have been obtained.

“Even if the agents and the analysts and the employees are sophisticated, you worry about their families too,” she said.

In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it said were false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”

That advisory characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was “offended” by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. It did not say what would happen if the FBI did not do so within a week.

“This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated,” the hacking group's message said.

ShinyHunters has a reputation for “causing trouble and being disruptive,” Wugmeister said, as evidenced by the group’s involvement in a hack last spring of Canvas, an online system used by thousands of schools and universities. The breach created chaos as students tried to study for finals and prompted the FBI’s advisory that ShinyHunters is now objecting to.

There have been other cyber incidents concerning the FBI

The hack was first reported by 404 Media, an online technology publication that said a representative of ShinyHunters shared what appeared to be a sample of personal data of 5,000 FBI employees, including addresses, phone numbers and some information on spouses.

The publication said the ShinyHunters representative said the group carried out the hack through an apparent vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft software, commonly used by companies and government agencies for large-scale data processing and human resources purposes. The FBI said in its statement that it had not determined whether the “point of breach” involved a “third-party or the FBI’s enterprise.”

The FBI, the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, has been a common target for hackers.

In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appeared to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.

The FBI described the compromised information as “historical in nature” and said it involved "no government information.”

entries.title: Court Filing Says Kennedy Center Hazards Prompted Closing, Not Trump’s Threats
entries.summary: The center’s executive director said the center could reopen once safety issues are addressed.
entries.content:
Kennedy Center officials said in a court filing Wednesday that the shuttered building could reopen once major safety hazards detailed in a new report are fixed — even as President Donald Trump has cast the center’s future on whether he gets his name engraved on the landmark.

The status report filed by the Justice Department in federal court offers a narrower explanation for the shutdown than Trump’s warning that the center could end up “ripped down” if he is not recognized on the building.

A sworn declaration from Executive Director Matt Floca details several “hazard and life-safety concerns,” including collapsing ceiling panels, water-infiltrating electrical transformers and concerns about unsafe theater equipment, but contains no finding that the center needs to be demolished.

The center’s Trump-appointed board voted last week to close the venue during the $250 million renovations. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) is fighting the closure in her role as an ex officio board member, arguing that the shutdown violates an existing court order from Judge Christopher R. Cooper and could be a pretext for something permanent.

Floca said he extended the temporary closure for another week “to protect employees, patrons, artists, contractors, and other members of the public while the Center evaluated documented falling-object hazards and other infrastructure conditions and determined what measures would be required for safe occupancy and emergency egress,” according to the report.

The filing included new details about the building’s condition, centering around the severe storms that pummeled D.C. earlier this month, in which “a large section of ceiling plaster weighing approximately 150 pounds fell from approximately 60 feet to the floor in a public thoroughfare.”

Water apparently also made its way into an electrical transformer vault, according to a Tuesday inspection by WB Engineers+Consultants. The contractor also discovered concrete fragments and other debris on the equipment, according to the court filing.

Staff also flagged problems with opera house lighting supports and counterweight rigging systems.

Floca said that the emergency shutdown is separate from the board’s longer-term closure plan. Wednesday’s filing says interim safeguards would not resolve the underlying deterioration or determine the scope or duration of a larger renovation.

After the center’s board approved the closure, Trump asserted that renovations would stay off the table altogether unless he received a favorable court decision.

“The Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on Truth Social.

The court filing provides no firm reopening date.

Beatty’s attorneys did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s requests for comment.

entries.title: Republicans Break With Trump After Immigration Crackdowns Hit Home
entries.summary: Republicans are signaling they see it as a vulnerability in some of the country’s most competitive races.
entries.content:
Several Republican candidates in competitive races are criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, signaling that they see it as a vulnerability in a political landscape that seems poised to favor Democrats.

The immigration agenda, a hallmark of President Donald Trump’s campaigns, has led to major deportation operations across the country — including in some of the states where Republicans are actively breaking with him on the issue.

Just this week, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican running for Congress in the state’s competitive 2nd Congressional District, told reporters that ICE should prioritize “people in the gangs and criminals first” while sharing that his son’s father-in-law is currently facing deportation despite holding a work permit.

“He came from a country that's not to the liking of certain people in Washington,” LePage said at a press conference in Augusta, Maine, on Monday, but didn’t say more about the man. “That’s not right.”

LePage’s campaign did not respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment. The state where LePage is running was the site of an immigration enforcement operation in January. In July, federal immigration agents shot a man in Biddeford, Maine, and prompted Republican Sen. Susan Collins to call on Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to cease all non-essential traffic stops in the state. The administration did, until Trump reversed the decision.

Several issues are causing rifts between the White House and Republican candidates, particularly those in tough races. Earlier this week, for example, two Republicans — Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson and Michigan senate candidate Mike Rogers — called for a swift end to the president’s war in Iran.

Immigration has been a similar lightning rod, and Democrats are on the offensive over it. They see the administration’s policies on immigration as an issue that will move voters towards their party come November.

The Trump administration has implemented a large-scale mass deportation campaign that has involved sweeping enforcement with a historic amount of funding going toward the Department of Homeland Security, and more than 610,000 people across the country detained since the president’s inauguration last January, according to The Marshall Project.

The Trump administration has increasingly restricted pathways of legal immigration as well, resulting in many people losing their legal status and protections. The aggressive immigration tactics appear to be posing a problem for candidates as the midterms inch closer.

The Republican who has perhaps been the most direct in criticizing the president’s immigration agenda is from Florida. Rep. María Elvira Salazar released an ad last week criticizing Trump’s immigration policies.

Salazar, who is also running in a competitive district, warned Trump that “some of your immigration enforcements have gone too far.” “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” the lawmaker, who represents a heavily Latino and immigrant district, continued.

Texas Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is rated “lean Republican” by Cook Political Report, put out an ad earlier this month featuring the story of a DACA recipient who was detained by ICE. The ad suggests that De La Cruz helped release the man from detention.

De La Cruz’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Her state has also seen high-profile consequences of Trump’s immigration agenda play out, including ICE officers shooting a man in Austin over the weekend. The man’s lawyer told CNN he is facing partial paralysis. That incident happened just two months after officers fatally shot a man in Houston.

The White House did not comment on the Republicans distancing themselves from Trump.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said he understood Salazar’s position, but that he just doesn’t “happen to be there.”

“She’s got a little bit soft on the border,” Trump, who has endorsed Salazar’s reelection bid, said. “I understand that.”

While those three candidates mark recent breaks in the party, at least one other vulnerable Republican has been holding the immigration aspect of the Trump agenda at arm’s length for longer.

New York Rep. Mike Lawler, who is running in one of the most competitive districts in the nation and who like Salazar and De La Cruz voted for last summer’s spending bill that gave record-level funding to DHS, has also praised the president’s high number of deportations. But he has called for DHS to reassess its tactics.

“Americans are increasingly concerned about the Department of Homeland Security’s enforcement operations,” Lawler wrote in an op-ed published in The New York Times following fatal shootings by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis. His campaign referred The Sun to the op-ed.

In an ad that first aired last week, Lawler touted his support for the Dignity Act — a bill co-sponsored by Salazar that would create steps through which long-term undocumented immigrants would be able to apply for legal status.

“I’m working hard on the Dignity Act, so that everyone can reach the American Dream,” Lawler said in Spanish in the ad.

entries.title: How Progressive Powerhouses Put Their Endorsements to Work
entries.summary: The high-profile support can drive millions to candidates, but the timing makes a difference according to The Washington Sun’s analysis.
entries.content:
The older crowd may be on the outs for progressive Democrats, but if younger candidates want a campaign boost, the left wing’s old guard is where to turn first, a Washington Sun analysis of high-profile progressive endorsers finds.

It also found differing strategies in how the leading figures on the left decide when to formally bless aspirants to the U.S. House and Senate.

The analysis, which crunched data on endorsements from a number of leading figures on the left and subsequent donations from the endorsers’ networks in the current election cycle, found that through July 31 donors in Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders’ network contributed the most, followed by that of California Rep. Ro Khanna.

The Sanders imprimatur spurred his backers to dole out $9.1 million to 21 chosen candidates, for an average of more than $433,000, though the largest amount, $3.1 million went to the now-defunct Senate campaign of Maine’s Graham Platner. Khanna backed 15 congressional hopefuls, enticing his network to hand out an average of $227,000 to each campaign for a total of $3.4 million.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/jyU5U/1/Among high-profile Democrats like Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York) and Ilhan Omar (Michigan), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Massachusetts), Warren has generated the most endorsements and donations, picking 11 congressional candidates and helping generate nearly $2.7 million, an average of more than $242,000 per candidate.

Ocasio-Cortez and Omar have been more conservative in naming favorites. Before the analysis’ July 31 cut off, the New York representative anointed seven candidates, who received $1.8 million from her network for an average of over $257,000. Omar threw her support behind nine candidates who landed nearly $1.6 million, or just under $174,000 a piece.

The data also reveal differing strategies, with Sanders and Khanna taking a riskier endorse-often and endorse-early approach. Sanders’ backing came a median of 103 days before his choices’ primaries. Khanna’s median is 96. Warren’s median endorsement date is also a relatively long 82 days ahead of time.

In the case of Khanna, who harbors national ambitions but isn’t as well-known, the early aid can be helpful in raising his profile and building gratitude with up and coming progressives. He’s also backed numerous non-federal candidates. In Sanders’ case, it marks a shift, said Julian Mulvey, one of the architects of Sanders’ first presidential campaign.

He told The Washington Sun it once “took a long time” for candidates to earn the Vermont senator’s support, but “that’s changed” with this cycle’s slate of endorsements. He praised Sanders and Khanna for their aggressive strategies, which helped raise resources and the profiles of left-leaning candidates who have won primaries.

Sanders supporters like Mulvey acknowledged the risk of a shoot-fast-and-early endorsement strategy. Platner is the prime example, having soared to prominence with help from the millions Sanders’ donors forked over only to drop his bid in July amid allegations of sexual assault. Sanders endorsed Platner 283 days before his primary victory in June, and stood by the oysterman through numerous earlier flare ups before calling for Platner to quit after assault allegations became public.

Neither Ocasio-Cortez nor Omar ever endorsed Platner.

They wait until late, functioning more like closers in the final innings of primaries. Omar has endorsed candidates less than a month before their primaries — a median of 29 days. For Ocasio-Cortez, it’s just 20 days before the election.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/KIZxv/1/While the slower endorsements could be seen as a sort of Johnny-come-lately caution, it can also reflect the extraordinary — and often hostile — attention directed at the pair, especially at Ocasio-Cortez.

“I don’t think anyone can quite appreciate the astonishing level of scrutiny that falls on her, it is like no one else in the party,” Mulvey said about Ocasio-Cortez. “I give her a tremendous amount of leeway to figure this out, because no one else has to face that level or scrutiny. I don’t blame her at all for being very careful, very judicious.”

The later endorsements also have the effect of delivering a more concentrated stream of cash that comes in over a compressed time frame, perhaps when it’s needed most.

For instance, Sanders backed the Senate campaign of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan a full 474 days before the primary, and Khanna followed with an endorsement just a week later. Sanders supporters contributed nearly $2.1 million to El-Sayed after the endorsement, and Khanna’s network added just shy of $1 million.

Ocasio-Cortez endorsed El-Sayed just 33 days before his primary, and Omar threw her support behind the Michigan progressive 22 days before the election as the race was tightening. In the time after the endorsements, Ocasio-Cortez donors gave El-Sayed over $940,000 and Omar’s network contributed almost $735,000.

Another progressive strategist said the endorsements from Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and other leaders in the movement, no matter when they come through, are needed to capitalize on an environment that is “very amenable to progressive challengers.”

“Organizing is great, but even that requires money,” the strategist said. “Because progressive voters are extremely invested, a little money goes a lot further with them.”

The Sun determined the impacts of the endorsers by analyzing federal campaign finance records to identify donors who contributed to the progressive congressional leaders over several election cycles, then calculating how much those donors contributed in the 2026 midterm cycle to the campaigns that each lawmaker endorsed. Donors were matched using normalized names and ZIP codes. The analysis also examined the timing of endorsements, including how far ahead of an election they were made and when a leader’s donors began giving to endorsed candidates. The analysis supplemented Federal Election Commission data with ActBlue earmarked contribution data to capture small-dollar donations that do not always appear individually in a candidate’s FEC filings.

entries.title: Trump’s Domestic Woes Are Growing. He’ll Throw Xi a Lavish Visit Anyway.
entries.summary: Crucial geopolitical negotiations — and lavish White House events — come as Trump navigates a sharp downturn in his second term.
entries.content:
When President Donald Trump welcomes President Xi Jinping of China to the White House on Thursday, it will be at a low point in his second term. Republicans are rebelling on issues that are personal to the president: an expensive gift to his son, a media ban, mass deportations, the Iran war — even Xi's visit. Polls and surveys show him with his lowest approval rating. Trump even seems to have given up on Republicans maintaining control of Congress in November’s midterms.

Meanwhile, Xi arrives preparing to lay the groundwork for his next five-year term, believing he’s visiting a nation in decline and granting Trump a visit the president has sought since before his second inauguration.

“There's a really unfortunate split screen here for the United States,” said Jonathan Czin, the director for China on the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden.

But as the fractions deepen within the Republican Party, Trump has turned his attention to reciprocating the reception he received in China earlier this year.

Although Trump greeted Xi when the Chinese president arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday — the first time since 1962 a president has personally welcomed a foreign leader at JBA — the summit truly kicks off Thursday with a lavish and meticulously planned day of events at the White House.

It's expected to be a continuation of Wednesday’s pageantry, when Xi stepped off his plane and onto a red carpet with a dozen fighter jets to his right, an artillery salute to his left and two B-1 bombers shrieking low overhead. But while some are dismayed by the extravagance, current and former U.S. officials and China policy experts say it is key to the success of the first Chinese state visit to Washington in 11 years.

Daniel R. Russel, who served as the assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during Xi’s 2015 state visit, told The Washington Sun the opulence is the cost of doing business with the Chinese, who he said are reluctant to travel to the U.S. without the prestige a state visit brings. It’s a projection of China’s superpower status, Russel added, even as it sees a distinctive change in its relationship with the U.S.

“The relationship is very different. A lot of it boils down to the shift in relative strength and leverage between Beijing and Washington,” Russel said. “The Chinese leadership is feeling very strong right now compared to the U.S., that they’ve got a considerable amount of leverage, a reasonable analysis of Trump and how to manipulate him.”

In May, a Chinese official told The Sun that the country spent weeks preparing for Trump’s visit to Beijing, a visit punctuated by pomp and circumstance at every event and interaction. Trump has sought to return the favor.

Last week on the White House grounds, reporters could see military rehearsals in anticipation of Xi’s arrival. The administration planned a multilayered welcome for Xi, with a ceremony that will move from the South Lawn to the state floor and the Rose Garden. A flyover by stealth aircraft will cap a military parade of 479 personnel for Xi and his wife, Madam Peng Liyuan. The day is scheduled to end with a state dinner curated by first lady Melania Trump and featuring some of America’s most powerful business leaders.

Melania Trump told Fox News on Wednesday that there were “a lot of details” to plan for a state dinner.

“There is protocol that you need to follow,” she said, adding she was involved in every detail.

An Obama-era official involved in planning the 2015 state dinner, Xi’s last in the U.S., said a dinner for the Chinese president brought heightened pressure compared with other foreign dignitaries.

“We had to be very precise about everything,” the Obama official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to speak freely. “And I mean that's every state dinner, but China, there is a history of a contentious relationship that we had to consider and make sure everything was to a T.”

Barack Obama, Xi Jinping 790376218435 (4004x2848, AR: 1.41)
Fearing they might accidentally insult the Chinese, the official said, “our main [goal] was to be so detailed … making sure that we didn't offend or do anything that would mess up any conversations or be a talking point later on.”

Some people aren’t pleased that Xi is here at all. Protesters forced the military to close an access point at JBA during Xi’s arrival. Others marched downtown Wednesday night chanting, “End the CCP!” And Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) denounced the visit during a floor speech on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio brushed off concerns about the displays. When asked by The Sun to respond to Wicker’s comments, Rubio defended the lavishness of Xi’s reception, saying that the relationship between the two nations would “define the 21st century.”

“The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It's outrageous,” Rubio said. “So we have, I think, an obligation to be able to interact and speak at the highest levels. And I think that's what this visit reflects, is the president's belief that no matter what our disagreements and differences may be with the Chinese government, this is not some small country.”

entries.title: Security Concerns Spur D.C. to Consider Privacy Protections for Judges
entries.summary: One federal judge is said to have received dozens of unsolicited pizza deliveries.
entries.content:
The D.C. Council is considering giving local and federal judges the ability to request that information about them — including their home address, personal phone numbers and the names of family members — be removed from public and private databases, a step that advocates say is needed to ensure their security in an era of increasing threats to jurists.

The bill, introduced by council Chair Phil Mendelson, would cover Supreme Court justices; federal judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals, U.S. District Court and U.S. Bankruptcy Court; and judges in D.C. Superior Court and the D.C. Court of Appeals. It would prohibit individuals, the government and businesses from disclosing judges’ personal information if a request is made that it not be shared.

The legislation was drafted at the request of Judge Robert Wilkins of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, who reached out to Mendelson in September 2024 to press the matter, indicating that he had been the victim of doxing. He noted that D.C. allows victims of domestic violence to shield their personal information, and asked that judges be offered the same opportunity.

“Unfortunately, there are people who want to use threats to intimidate judges, or even worse, to harm or kill judges as retribution for our rulings. Such actions are not just attacks on the individual judges, they are attacks on our system of justice and the rule of law itself,” Wilkins wrote in testimony submitted to the council ahead of a hearing Wednesday.

Wilkins recounted a number of local cases of judges being threatened or killed, including Maryland Circuit Court Judge Andrew Wilkinson, who was shot and killed in 2023 by a man whose divorce proceedings he was overseeing. The killing spurred legislative action to protect judges’ privacy in Maryland; Mendelson’s bill is modeled after what Maryland lawmakers approved.

Wilkins also cited threats faced by Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and an incident this year at the home of Justice Amy Coney Barrett where someone called 911 and falsely reported gunshots in hopes of provoking a large police response. Wilkins also said one of his own colleagues had been subject to dozens of unsolicited pizza deliveries in D.C.

“Officials with the U.S. Marshals Office tell me that there have been at least 64 recent incidents when a pizza was delivered to the home of one of our D.C. federal judges by a stranger, and many of those deliveries came with a message referencing Judge Esther Salas, a federal judge whose husband and son were shot at the front door of her New Jersey home in 2020, by a disgruntled litigant posing as a delivery man,” he wrote.

An August report from the University of California, Berkeley, and New York University law schools found that while criticism of the courts and individual judicial decisions are part and parcel of a democracy, intensifying political polarization has taken those disagreements to a more troubling level.

“Threats of violence, intimidation, and disinformation directed at judges, and defiance of court orders go beyond healthy criticism and fundamentally threaten judicial independence,” said the report. “Attacks of this nature are not new. But in recent years, the experience of federal judges and data indicate that the frequency and severity of such attacks have escalated significantly.”

Those sorts of attacks and threats can be distinctly present in D.C., Wilkins told Mendelson in his original letter in late 2024 requesting legislative action.

“We handle numerous cases of national interest and which spur heated controversy, including all of the criminal cases from the January 6, 2021 insurrection,” he wrote.

Congress adopted a federal law to better shield judges’ personal information in late 2022, and this summer Barrett and Justice Elena Kagan testified before Congress on the need for more security for judges. Still, Wilkins and other advocates say that state-level action is also necessary.

While the D.C. bill has support, the devil will be in the details. Local supporters of Mendelson’s bill say it will need to simplify the process for judges in D.C. to request that their personal information be removed from public and private databases.

“Suppose a judge buys a home, registers to vote, enrolls her children in public school, applies for a permit to build a fence around her home, and calls 311 to have the remains of her old fence picked up as bulk trash. That judge’s home address is now in the databases of at least six different D.C. agencies,” said Misty Thomas Zaleski of the Council for Court Excellence.

While the majority of the threats have been faced by federal judges, Doug Buchanan, a spokesperson for D.C.’s local courts, said it would similarly provide local judges “some added security barriers between the judiciary and those that they serve.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Attacks on Judges
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 24, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Shored-up security for D.C. judges, jury deliberations in the Trayon White trial and your burning Nationals questions, answered.

Capital Weather's Daily Digit: — 6/10: Partial sunshine feels like a big win after several days dominated by rain and clouds.

THE LATEST

Having 64 unsolicited pizza deliveries to your home may sound like a quirky prank, but for some judges, it can feel like an unsettling threat.

That’s what some federal judges in D.C. have faced in recent years, as increasing political polarization and fights over judicial rulings have led to a spike in threats and intimidation — including at their homes.

“Such actions are not just attacks on the individual judges, they are attacks on our system of justice and the rule of law itself,” Judge Robert Wilkins of the U.S. Court of Appeals in D.C. wrote in testimony delivered to the D.C. Council on Wednesday.

The council is considering a bill that would offer local and federal judges in D.C. increased security by way of privacy, The Washington Sun's Martin Austermuhle reports. It would allow them to request that personal information be removed from public and private databases, including their home address, phone number and relatives’ names.

Maryland approved a similar bill after the 2023 slaying of Maryland Circuit Court Judge Andrew Wilkinson by a man whose divorce proceedings he was overseeing. Congress passed its own version in late 2022, but Wilkins and other advocates say more state-level action is needed to close gaps and increase enforcement.

Speaking to Congress this summer, Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett — herself the victim of a “swatting” incident when someone called 911 with a false report of a shooting at her Virginia home — advocated for more security for judges.

While similar measures are being considered elsewhere, Wilkins explained that D.C.-based judges can face even more threats because of the politically charged cases they often have to deal with. “We handle numerous cases of national interest and which spur heated controversy, including all of the criminal cases from the January 6, 2021 insurrection,” he explained in a late-2024 letter asking for the council to act.





FROM THE COURTHOUSE

The jury began deliberating in the bribery trial of Ward 8 council member Trayon White. Proceedings were largely quiet, but prosecutors did file a notice alleging that a member of the public spoke improperly to an alternate juror who had been dismissed ahead of deliberations.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Mark Zuckerberg, a higher property tax bill may be coming your way. Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin has unveiled a bill that would impose a new pied-à-terre tax for homes in D.C. owned by wealthy individuals who don’t live in the city full-time. (Zuckerberg bought a $23 million mansion in Woodland Normanstone in 2025.) The new tax rate would only hit an estimated 600 properties but would bring in an estimated $130 million over four years. Members of Congress and federal appointees would be exempted. Frumin’s bill comes ahead of a mid-October council hearing on possible tax increases to cover a large estimated budget gap next year.

About 80 landlords are expected to testify today in a housing committee hearing weighing a blockbuster bill that would (among many other things) speed up the eviction process by setting a 60-day initial hearing deadline. Landlords hope it’s the first step in rolling back some of the pandemic-era protections they say “devastated” their industry and enabled a vicious cycle of tenant nonpayment and buildings falling into disrepair.

In a similar vein, at a judiciary and public safety committee hearing yesterday, 10 landlords testified on a bill that would help evict squatters in short-term housing; they asked that council members extend that idea to long-term housing, too.

Meanwhile, homeless encampments in D.C. have largely disappeared a year after President Donald Trump pushed a crackdown, The Sun’s Raymond Fernández reports. Homelessness is still, however, a major problem in the District, with no permanent solutions in sight.

Trump is not considering adding his name to Ford’s Theatre as part of his push to put his mark on the city, contrary to an MS NOW report, the Interior Department told The Sun’s Kendall Staton.





FROM VIRGINIA

The Loudoun County School Board adopted a religiously diverse calendar for the 2028-29 school year, as opposed to one based on the federal holiday calendar that only includes major Christian holidays, by a 5-4 vote and after a contentious debate, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Gov. Wes Moore signed an executive order Wednesday imposing stricter regulations on data center development in the state, The Sun’s Raymond Fernández reports. Maryland joins a broader bipartisan effort that is taking place across the country, in which states — citing federal inaction — are trying to regulate data centers through executive action.





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

I want to try Ethiopian for the first time. Where should I go?

Silver Spring. That’s where you’ll find Beteseb Restaurant and a physical menu shaped like a round of injera with colorful photos of some of the dishes you can order. (Injera, you’re about to discover, is both a sour, sponge-like flatbread and a utensil for wrapping around Ethiopian stews and salads.)



The 50-seat storefront is nicely dressed with walls in a shade of yellow lentils and a silver-toned silhouette of Addis Ababa. The signatures include a dynamite vegetarian sampler and kitfo, Ethiopia’s fiery answer to steak tartare, as well as a favorite dish of mine: boiled, ground beef tripe spiked with jalapeño, the spice blend mitmita and cardamom.

Beteseb translates from Amharic to “family,” which is pretty much how the staff makes you feel while dining there.

For more from Tom, check out this week’s Talk to Tom Q&A.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: How Progressives Grow Their Power
entries.content:
Today’s notice: White House access is back. A nitty-gritty look at the political strategy of the populist left. D.C.’s homeless problem after the Trump law enforcement surge. More on the seniority war in the House Democratic Caucus. Ballroom money questions. And: Lee Greenwood’s royalty checks. 





THE LATEST

Breaking overnight: Federal Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” press credentials to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

“Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote in the 14-day temporary restraining order.

How the Democrats’ new kingmakers get it done: Endorsements from prominent, nationwide progressives — like Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), or Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and Ro Khanna (D-California) — carry outsize weight in the modern Democratic Party. As we look ahead to the midterms and beyond, it’s helpful to learn the similarities and differences among these modern power players’ endorsement strategies.

The Washington Sun’s Stephen Neukam crunched the numbers and found some interesting results. Sanders and Khanna endorsed early this cycle, a median of around 100 days out from primaries. Warren’s median was 82 days. AOC’s stamp of approval was much closer to the primary date.

In Michigan, for example, Sanders and Khanna endorsed the eventual Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, more than 400 days before the primary election, while AOC popped her endorsement 33 days before.

What it means to get these endorsements: Progressive politicians’ networks give — and give big, Stephen writes. He’s got charts, too. They show that donors who have already contributed to the likes of Sanders or AOC dig deep and give again to the candidates they back. The result is not the huge sums a single billionaire can drop into a race, but rather a steady stream of smaller dollars that have turned progressive challengers into primary winners.

“Organizing is great, but even that requires money,” one Democratic strategist told The Sun. “Because progressive voters are extremely invested, a little money goes a lot further with them.”

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Actually, from Joint Base Andrews: It was quite a sight to behold when Donald Trump greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping when Xi’s plane touched down for his first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade. The Sun’s Ben T.N. Mause was there and reports a military cordon stood at attention alongside American dignitaries in front of a sprawling phalanx of F-22 and F-16 fighter jets, as B-1 bombers circled overhead. Tonight is a state dinner and, if one can imagine it, even more diplomatic pomp.

More: China Is Holding Sensitive F-35 Parts That Were Meant to Be Shipped to the U.S. • Trump Administration Publicly Invites Putin to Attend the G20 Summit

FROM THE DISTRICT


Homelessness after the Trump takeover: There are fewer large encampments, but the city’s homelessness problem remains as challenging as ever. The Sun’s Raymond Fernández spoke to policymakers, advocates and people living on the streets about what a year of presidential attention to the issue has meant. “It’s not just like we’re out here randomly,” one woman living outside D.C.’s MLK Memorial Library, a site that has become less welcoming to her, said.

FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Committee chair squeeze: We’ve already told you about House Democrats beginning to hash out new rules for managing the chamber if they win control in November. The latest idea from some in the caucus: making dues payments to the DCCC a requirement to hold a House committee chair. The Sun’s Kadia Goba and Oriana González report that this esoteric idea — chairs are currently encouraged to pay the dues — is actually another sign of bubbling caucus frustration over seniority that could bedevil a possible Democratic majority next year.

“It’s crazy that these chairs do nothing to get the majority and sit back and expect that because they have always been, they will always be,” one House Democrat fumed.

FROM THE HILL


First on The Sun: Democrat wants ballroom funding answers. Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-New Hampshire) is asking the U.S. Secret Service how the reported diversion of more than $350 million dollars from its budget to Trump’s ballroom has impacted the service’s operations.

In a letter obtained by The Sun, Hassan writes to USSS Director Sean Curran asking if the money’s rerouting has altered “the ability of the Secret Service to carry out its essential responsibilities to protect the President as well as to safeguard the U.S. financial infrastructure.”

Trump said yesterday the ballroom itself is ahead of schedule.

“The entire left portion, the north portion, has been built structurally, and it will start to be covered up now with very powerful glass,” the president boasted. “It’s going to be something.”

FROM AUDI FIELD


The politicians who play ball with the press: The annual Congressional Women’s Softball Game last night was a high-scoring affair that, as usual, pit members of Congress against journalists. As it should be, the Bad News Babes beat Team Congress like a drum, with the final score of 22-16. The Sun’s Manuela Silva was in the stands and reports that Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) was the MVP of the congressional team and the squad was cheered on from the sidelines by Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California). There were also free McNuggets and Georgetown Cupcakes.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Lee Greenwood’s payday: The musician’s spouse was nominated to be ambassador to Barbados, so The Sun’s Dave Levinthal looked at her required disclosure forms. What he found was just how lucrative the song “God Bless the USA” has been for Lee Greenwood — he earned up to $1 million in recent months from royalties paid for the tune, which is a regular at Trump events.

Less lucrative was the version recorded about Canada, which Greenwood produced at George H.W. Bush’s behest in 1989. That one only brought in up to $1,000 in recent royalties.

entries.title: The Trump Administration Has Made It Harder to Be Homeless in D.C.
entries.summary: Unhoused populations are being pushed — little by little and with nowhere else to go — from one location to another.
entries.content:
Homelessness encampments in D.C. have largely disappeared a year after President Donald Trump pushed a crackdown. Homelessness is still, however, a major problem in the city.

If anything, the combination of Trump’s pressure to push unhoused people out of the capital and Mayor Muriel Bowser’s response have made struggles worse, according to local lawmakers and advocates for D.C.’s homeless population.

“Trump's presence here has really exacerbated what's already a challenging local issue,” said D.C. Council member Brianne Nadeau, who chaired the Committee on Human Services from 2017 to 2022.

“Under Trump two specifically, Mayor Bowser has tended to comply in advance, in which case, sometimes [proper] protocols are not followed,” Nadeau added, pointing to the clearing of a small encampment by Washington Circle in August of last year as an example.

Effectively, this has translated to unhoused populations being pushed — little by little and with nowhere permanent to go — from one location to another.

Many homeless people are even less sure about their future in the changing city. In August 2025, Trump posted to Truth Social that “The Homeless have to move out, IMMEDIATELY. We will give you places to stay, but FAR from the Capital.”
DC Federal Intervention (5113x3409, AR: 1.50)In the months since, the District has seen a significant decrease in encampments across the city. In July, the city’s Department of Health and Human Services closed twice as many encampments as it did during the same month last year, while homelessness increased by 4.4% from the previous year, according to the district’s Point-In-Time count.

The White House did not address the effect of the administrations’ actions, whether federal resources had been made available to the people displaced by encampment removals or advocates’ concerns in response to an inquiry from The Washington Sun.

“The crackdown on encampments is NOT linked to a rise in homelessness,” Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House, said in a statement.

The Bowser administration referred The Sun to the Office of the Deputy Mayor for Health and Human Services, which oversees housing issues.

In a statement, a city spokesperson said that federal intervention has not affected outreach efforts in the District, adding that encampment removal procedures have remained “consistent.”

“Whether a resident has been impacted by one, or numerous closures, does not alter our efforts to engage with them, establish a relationship, and make connections to shelter and services,” said a spokesperson for the deputy mayor’s office in a statement.

The Bowser administration, the statement continued, believes that “the safest place for people is in a shelter or permanent housing,” pointing to bridge housing facilities, which provide rooms and personalized case management to people experiencing homelessness, and other shelters.

But this crackdown, in addition to a lack of funding, has created a new set of issues for the city and its homeless population, according to some of the groups who try to serve it.

“People are less trusting, and they're less willing to share their name, and they're less willing to give any identifying information and to engage in services because they are scared,” said Andrew Wassenich, the director of the policy advocacy team at Miriam's Kitchen.
IMG_9795 copy.jpg (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)These changes are visible outside of places like Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library in Northwest D.C., which has been a destination for people experiencing homelessness over the years.

One woman, a 53-year-old who requested anonymity out of privacy concerns, said she has slept outside the library since February. She said she makes $15,000 a year in disability benefits and has been waiting on two apartment applications that she hopes will get her off the street.

She likes the library. She appreciates that there is often security nearby, especially at night. And she hopes that she can stay there until she secures housing.

“It's not just like we're out here randomly,” the woman told The Sun.

“Some people are really trying to get housed,” the woman said. “The [library] is kind of safe because the programs are here. There's counselors that come out, and they're routinely out here.”

But in July of this year, the MLK library announced it would revamp a police presence outside the building and even set up a dividing rope to clear a sheltered area outside of the library.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

In a statement to The Sun, a spokesperson for D.C. Public Library argued that “conditions in that area have created a barrier to participation at the MLK Library,” explaining that the measures were put in place in response to community members' concerns.

“Even with daily cleaning, the area under the loggia has become unwelcoming,” George Williams, D.C. Public Library’s media relations manager, said, in reference to the covered area where many homeless people used to congregate in.

Among advocates for ending homelessness, the frustration with the federal and local government is hard to hide.

“People are trapped in homelessness because elected officials — both at the D.C. level and at the federal level — are not prioritizing the needs of people experiencing homelessness,” Jesse Rabinowitz, campaigns and communications director at the National Homelessness Law Center, told The Sun.

“Magically, the government found hundreds of millions of dollars to deploy the National Guard, including to get folks into housing,” Rabinowitz said. “They can pay for housing when they want to.”

entries.title: No Dues, No Gavel: House Democrats Float Forcing Committee Leaders Pay Up
entries.summary: “It’s crazy that these chairs do nothing to get the majority,” one House Democrat told The Sun.
entries.content:
Some House Democrats are pushing a caucus rule change that would make paying campaign dues a condition for any lawmaker seeking posts as committee and subcommittee leaders, The Washington Sun has learned.

After the lawmakers return to the Capitol after the midterms, some Democrats plan to bring up a proposal in their organizational meetings for next Congress that would ensure committee leaders are contributing dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — the political and fundraising apparatus that assists caucus-wide members in their reelection bids.

Democrats are expected to contribute to the party's fundraising arm, and leaders establish a scale of dues each election cycle, ranging from a low six-figure range for rank-and-file members to $1.1 million for those serving in leadership and on top-tier committees, like Ways and Means or Appropriations.

Currently, paying dues to the DCCC is encouraged but not required. But of the 21 House Democrats who currently serve as committee ranking members, seven have paid half or less what they owe, according to an August dues report obtained by The Sun.

The change is among a number of demands Democratic members are angling for if they take back the majority, including requiring term limits for committee leadership roles.

“There is a recognition that we want our leaders to be in good standing, and that includes doing everything possible to ensure a House Democratic majority,” Rep. Mike Levin of California, chair of the House Democratic Committee on Caucus Rules, told The Sun. The committee works with members to write proposals that can then be brought to the entire caucus for a vote.

Levin said the proposal, which has not been finished, would lay out what qualifies a chair as “member in good standing.”

The standard of “in good standing,” Levin said, would include the member paying DCCC dues, attending House votes and voting with the rest of the caucus on procedural votes. The latter requirement is in direct response to Reps. Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington state voting with Republicans to advance two procedural votes earlier this month. That move prompted Democrats to demand that leadership formally reprimand them.

“It’s crazy that these chairs do nothing to get the majority and sit back and expect that because they have always been, they will always be,” one House Democrat, granted anonymity to speak frankly, told The Sun.

Lawmakers have privately denounced Reps. Bobby Scott of Virginia and Maxine Waters of California, the top Democrats on the Education and Workforce and Financial Services committees, respectively, as two people who, they argue, regularly don’t pay their dues.

The latest report shows Scott paid 100% of his DCCC dues as of August, a significant increase from the 9% he had paid back in April, according to a dues report from that month. In the spring, Virginia Democrats were campaigning for a redistricting referendum, which ultimately failed, that would have helped Democrats gain more seats in the House. In a statement to The Sun, Scott indicated that was why his April numbers were lagging.

“My number-one focus right now is helping to elect at least 218 Democrats to win back the majority. I campaigned for the Virginia Redistricting Referendum earlier this year, and now I am working to flip at least 3 seats in the Commonwealth. I have paid my dues in full, as I have always done, and I have contributed to Frontline Members and all the Red to Blue candidates,” Scott said in the statement.

On the other hand, Waters has only paid 15% of her dues for this election cycle. Her office did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, asked if he backs barring members from seeking leadership positions if they haven’t paid their dues, said, “Well, it’s all hands on deck right now. And we continue to encourage every single member of the House Democratic Caucus to be as supportive as they can.”

Democrats, Jeffries added at a Wednesday news conference, have continued to “narrowly” outraise Republicans this cycle “and we need to continue to keep that pace going forward.” He insisted that Democrats will have the resources they need to win in November.

When reached for comment on this story, DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said, “appreciate you asking, but gonna have to politely decline to comment because we are busy working on winning the 2026 election.”

In the last few months, there’s been a rush of members playing catchup by making large contributions after previously being delinquent.

Members have taken notice. One source familiar with the matter said they witnessed a round of congratulatory text messages acknowledging Reps. Rick Larsen of Washington, Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon and Bennie Thompson of Mississippi had paid in full. Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey, who could see a challenge as the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, has, as of August, paid 100% of the $660,000 he was required to pay.

Larsen, the top Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, had paid 38% of his DCCC dues in April. By August, he had paid 83%. Similarly, Bonamici had paid 64% in April, but contributed more, meeting 82% of her dues level in August.

There are questions around how exactly a proposal to change caucus rules for fundraising would work, and if it can have any real teeth.

For instance, there are rules that require members to strictly separate their official legislative duties from their campaign and political work. Some House Democrats are concerned about linking a political responsibility such as paying campaign dues to performing a legislative role — being a committee leader.

“My prediction is that moving [forward], members are going to look back and see who has paid their dues in full and who hasn’t met their expectations,” said a second House Democrat who was skeptical the caucus would pass a rule targeting leaders. Anyone who has not met “their minimum in the past,” they added, has “got to be scrutinized more thoroughly.”

“That’s the strongest form of enforcement possible,” the lawmaker continued.

Three sources familiar with the process told The Sun the measure would be implemented if it gets a majority of the caucus behind it.

It’s also unclear how the measure would work when members in competitive districts, who the DCCC calls “frontliners” and who do not have to pay dues to the committee, run for committee leadership positions. For example, Rep. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut, running in a competitive district, is planning to challenge Virginia’s Scott to lead the Education and Workforce committee.

“I can't help that I live in a district that's a frontline district, and that presupposes that anyone who is a frontliner, we're just there to help deliver the majority and be cheerleaders,” Hayes told The Sun. “Democrats talk about candidate quality and the people that we recruit and how we are broadening our perspectives and bringing in different voices, that also will have to mean bringing those voices to the leadership table.”

Hayes said that she would support a dues-paying requirement: “There has to be some buy-in as part of the team, but also getting this work done isn’t just about your capacity to raise money.”

The push to require high-ranking committee members to pay doesn’t come without pushback. Newer members — especially those who have sworn off corporate PAC money — have complained about struggling to pay dues. Members in less affluent districts could also face barriers that would cause them to fall short of their dues obligations.

But the proposal could get enough votes to be adopted by the House Democratic Caucus in November, judging by how often members said the issue has come up in listening sessions the caucus’ rules committee has held.

“The vocal support has definitely outweighed any vocal opposition,” California’s Levin said.

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Where to Eat in Georgetown
entries.summary: Plus: What to do about extra charges on menus, and Ethiopian recommendations for a first-timer.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

What’s up with the extra charges on menus these days? Just give me honest menu prices!

Few things upset diners more right now than getting a bill with items they didn’t order — the credit card processing fee here and the “kitchen wellness” surcharge there. The terminology for surcharges isn’t standardized and customers are often left to wonder what the real cost of their meal is going to be.

Restaurateurs say they want to be transparent with customers, since the cost of food, labor — everything, really — has gone up. Diners tell me they feel nickel-and-dimed by what they see on their check.

I sympathize with both camps.

There are several reasons operators don’t want to simply raise menu prices. One, they want customers to know exactly where a fee is going, meaning it’s for something specific. (Businesses pay about 2% to 3% of a credit card transaction, for instance.) Two, they worry about how a price change affects competition from nearby restaurants and delivery services. Three, changing prices means reprinting menus, updating websites and other systems.

Ultimately, no restaurant wants to be the first on its block to charge $40 for roast chicken.

“I think there is a distrust of restaurants generally and a lack of respect as a blue-collar industry which puts us in this situation,” says veteran D.C. chef Amy Brandwein of the neighboring Centrolina and Piccolina in CityCenter. “Other industries decide their prices and consumers don’t analyze the cost of an iPhone, for example. Because food is something that most people can ‘make’ it leads to an unfair comparison.”

How can we put a stop to restaurants that send out entrées on the heels of appetizers?

Aren’t we all tired of places where servers ask diners to order everything at once, “so the chef can course things out,” only to have the whole shebang come out at once?

Been there, hated that.

One way to head off the problem is to politely tell your server from the start you’d prefer the main course be brought after you’ve finished your appetizer. Then, if your entrée arrives prematurely, say something immediately rather than accept the plate (which can cause a second problem by crowding the table).

Not long ago, I was at a restaurant where servers brought everything we ordered simultaneously, expecting us to make space for the pileup on a small table. Instead, I asked if the staff could return the entrées to the kitchen, because otherwise, we would have had to surrender a votive and flowers — part of the ambience — in the process. They complied.

There are exceptions based on expectations. Nobody supposes tapas purveyors or dim sum parlors — small plates specialists — should adhere to similar pacing, for instance.

I’m coming to town and staying in Georgetown. I’d like to eat there, too. 

You’re in luck. The historic neighborhood, which lost some of its appeal as a place to eat over the years as hot spots opened in Penn Quarter, 14th Street NW, Union Market, Shaw and elsewhere, is enjoying a second act as a dining destination in the District.

It was already home to a number of impressive restaurants: Chez Billy Sud for bistro fare, L’Avant-Garde and Lutèce for refined French, My Little Chamomile for Turkish, River Club for Italian/Lebanese/Spanish — fusion that works — and the Levantine-inspired Yellow café from the admired chef Michael Rafidi of Albi fame. The area has only gotten more appealing in recent seasons with the arrival of Ox & Olive for steak, Brasero Atlantico for Argentinean flavors and Alfie’s for northeastern Thai.
MyLittleChamomile_092326_151 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)MyLittleChamomile_092326_174.jpg (7795x5197, AR: 1.50)My most recent visits to Georgetown prompted me to put My Little Chamomile and L’Avant-Garde in my restaurant rotation. The former, from Turkish chef Cagla Onal-Urel, showcases small plates and a vegetable-driven menu. I like to go with a group to sample the lot. Double up on the Istanbul native’s sublime manti — sheer, beef-filled dumplings draped in tangy yogurt freckled with dried mint and sumac — and any new idea the chef picked up from her summer back home.

As for L’Avant-Garde, where Sébastien Giannini heads the kitchen, you can see where the owners poured $3 million to open several years ago. The low-ceiling bar and dining room are beauties. Picture ribs of wood stretching across the walls, cab-size semicircular booths, marble coasters for your drinks and lighting that flatters. The prized seats embrace a view of a crackling fire, an especially seductive touch as summer segues into fall. Among the standouts at dinner were a pastry-crowned lobster bouillabaisse and thin, golden veal cutlet finished with gribiche sauce and served with peerless french fries that nearly finished me. You can’t stop at one (or 10).

I want to try Ethiopian for the first time. Where should I go?

Silver Spring, Maryland. That’s where you’ll find Beteseb Restaurant and a physical menu shaped like a round of injera with colorful photos of some of the dishes you can order. (Injera, you’re about to discover, is both a sour, sponge-like flatbread and a utensil for wrapping around Ethiopian stews and salads.)

The 50-seat storefront is nicely dressed with walls in a shade of yellow lentils and a silver-toned silhouette of Addis Ababa. The signatures include a dynamite vegetarian sampler and kitfo, Ethiopia’s fiery answer to steak tartare, as well as a favorite dish of mine: boiled, ground beef tripe spiked with jalapeño, the spice blend mitmita and cardamom.

Beteseb translates from Amharic to “family,” which is pretty much how the staff makes you feel while dining there.

Hey Tom! I’m so glad to be able to enjoy your work again. Of the many server vocal tics we are enduring these days, the question “Are you still working on that?” particularly gets me steamed. It evokes such an awful image.

Copy that, servers? Consider this your PSA for the day.

There’s the option of simmering in silence, but if the question bothers you enough to write to me, you might consider (gently) correcting them with something that falls easier on your ears. As in, “Working sounds like a task, and this is joyful,” or, a cheekier approach: “Working is for field animals. But if you’re asking if I’m finished eating, yes, I am, thank you.” Said with a smile, the response serves as a playful correction.

There are plenty of polite ways for a server to ask if someone is done eating. “May I remove your plate?” is one. “May I take this out of your way?” and “Are you all set with this?” work better than “work,” too.

entries.title: How Sydney Johnson Helped Turn the Mystics Around
entries.summary: The second-year coach has helped transform Washington from basement dwellers to one of the WNBA’s most exciting — and dangerous — teams.
entries.content:
During a seven-game span in early August, Mystics guard Georgia Amoore totaled just 17 points. In four of those games she shot a combined zero for 10. Social media critics called for the former All-American, who missed the 2025 season with an ACL injury, to be benched.

Then, during a postgame conference on Aug. 15, Sydney Johnson, the Mystics’ head coach, was asked who the most underrated player on the team was. He immediately said Amoore, even though he knew it would “stir up a lot.”

Amoore wasn’t surprised, she said, because Johnson had shown her that level of compassion since she joined the team. But for her and her teammates, those small gestures go a long way.

“When the coach's belief in you is high, you know your belief in yourself is high and your teammates, and you know that can take you a really, really long way,” said Amoore, who since Aug. 19 has been averaging 11.6 points on 50.6% 3-point shooting for the Mystics, who enter the season’s final game Thursday as one of the WNBA’s most exciting and dangerous teams.

In just two seasons, Johnson has helped morph the Mystics from basement dwellers to a playoff team. From day one Johnson established his five pillars of team success: joy, direct communication, humility to work together, hard work and constant competition. The players embrace it and hold themselves accountable.

“I wasn't gonna let any riding the wave of wins, losses, injuries, officiating, a bad play call by me, I was not gonna let that steal the joy,” Johnson said. “And I was really, really committed to that.”

Part of that joy comes from establishing healthy relationships. Johnson talks to his players about not only basketball, but also life. Players feel that he cares and that they can be open, honest and direct without fear of consequence.

What’s been the result?

The top rebounding team (37.6 per game) in the league and the second-ranked scoring defense (82.5) allowing the second-lowest shooting percentage (43%), as of Sept. 23. Their 27-16 record is the sixth best in the league.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

For a team that was 16-27 at this same point last season, the turnaround in one year is impressive. It becomes staggering when you consider that Washington has the youngest roster in the league, eight of whom are rookies.

But the fact that the Mystics are ahead of schedule doesn’t limit their ambitions for what they’re capable of in this year’s playoffs, which begin this weekend.

“Since the beginning, we knew we had it in us and we wanted to get there,” star guard Sonia Citron said. “But at the same time, there's so many things we can get better at that we know there's even more potential.”

‘This Might Be a Little Different Group’


There wasn’t a single moment this season when Johnson knew he had something special.

Rather, the realization came during a pair of back-to-back games in the Bay.

In the first of consecutive games against the Valkyries at Chase Center in July, Washington led by six points with just over seven minutes remaining in the game. But Golden State got hot from the 3-point line and ended the game on a 15-4 run in a 74-69 win.

This was the Mystics’ first trip to San Francisco since last season when the Valkyries ran them off the floor in a 99-63 rout, handing Washington its sixth straight loss in what would end up being a 10-game losing streak. That memory was fresh as the Mystics headed into the second of the two games this season.

“I was very mindful of like, ‘Hey, we have to go out there, and of course we want to win, but we got to make sure that we play the way we know how to play — together and tough — and that we can't have our identity taken from us, we can't have our heart ripped out.”

The Valkyries, then on a nine-game winning streak, led 80-73 with three-and-a-half minutes left in the fourth quarter. A Shakira Austin steal and Cotie McMahon’s and-1 basket helped jump-start what would end up a 17-2 run that ended in a 90-82 Mystics win.

His team’s ability to shrug off the letdown from the first game and walk out of the second with an unflinching swagger was when Johnson was finally convinced.

“That's when I was like, ‘This might be a little different group.’”

Starting with the 2025 draft, the Mystics began a youth movement. They traded away veterans Ariel Atkins and Brittney Sykes while adding Citron, Kiki Iriafen and Amoore. Then last offseason, they emphasized getting bigger, faster and stronger. They drafted Lauren Betts, the 2026 NCAA tournament Final Four Most Outstanding Player, and McMahon, a two-time first-team All-Big Ten selection, while adding former rookie of the year Michaela Onyenwere and 2024 WNBA champion Betnijah Laney-Hamilton through free agency and off waivers, respectively.

Washington has allowed this core to learn on the job and play through their mistakes. While they didn’t always get the results they wanted, positive things came from the hard times.

“[Age] plays a factor, but it doesn't,” Citron said. “We don't want to use that as an excuse to say why we didn't win or why we didn't do what we wanted to do. It's because we're young. We don't think that's an excuse.”

Their youth may not be a crutch, but it is surely infectious. This TikTok generation of players has their 52-year-old coach acting differently.

How many people born during the Nixon presidency do you normally see doing the viral Scuba Dance? After victories, Johnson comes running into the locker room doing exaggerated acrobatics — all posted on social media, of course. Following Austin’s putback, and-1 game-winner over the Aces on July 22, Johnson ran in circles around the locker room before belly flopping onto the floor like he was Jimmy “Superfly” Snuka.

He’s asked if he felt the repercussions for that one the next day.

“People have asked me that. Honest, no,” Johnson said. “Maybe it was the adrenaline or something. I don't know, and I don't know what came over me or comes over me in those moments. But yeah, I'm still intact.”

Of course there’s the team’s self-created nickname that likely won’t be added to marketing materials anytime soon. All season the Mystics have been calling themselves the “Young Hos,” a play on their youngest-in-the-W age.

Johnson clutched his pearls at first but after further conversation with Iriafen and McMahon, he’s perfectly fine with how they choose to express themselves, as he’s encouraged them to.

“I think they're showing their genuine affection for each other, and I can't hold that back,” Johnson said. “The dad in me is like, ‘Be respectful and know that people have eyes on you.’ But it's really just the joy that they have for being around each other. So, I'm not going to stand in the way of that.”

‘It’s Time to Lock In’


There might be dance parties and “dubs in the chat,” but the Mystics know the goal is on-court success, not internet virality.

“We say some things or do some things that are just out of pocket and funny and, like, in the best way,” Amoore said. “But he'll laugh at it, and then when it's time to lock in, like, it's time to lock in.”

The team has been especially locked in on the defensive end. Iriafen (6-foot-3) and Austin (6-foot-5) are the imposing anchors, daring anyone to step foot in the paint at their own peril. Austin has held opponents to the second-lowest effective field goal percentage (51.1%) in the restricted area in the league, according to Second Spectrum, while both are in the top 10 in defensive rebound percentage. Citron is one of the peskiest wing defenders in the league, and if you give her even a millimeter she will step into a passing lane for an interception (her 1.2 steals per game leads the team).

“I love offense. I love pass, dribble, shoot. I love pace,” Johnson said. “But defensively, you’ve got to get stops. That's your toughness, that's your grit, and it shows your togetherness because it’s not a ton of stats on that. It's like we’ve got to work together.”

The offense, on the other hand, could use some work. They score the fourth-fewest points per game (82.6) and are bottom four in the league in 3-point attempts (19.5), makes (6.2) and percentage (31.9%).

Johnson said he sees offensive improvement in practice, it just hasn’t translated to games yet. The team puts Austin and Iriafen at the center of the scheme, which has translated to Washington averaging the third-most baskets (15.6) in the restricted area this season.

“We definitely play inside out and allow our strengths to come from the post, and using our size and using our athletic abilities,” Austin said.

That style might not be the most aesthetically pleasing, but it has allowed the Mystics to earn some tough victories. The last-minute win over the Valkyries. The last-second triumph over the reigning champion Aces. The four-overtime marathon win over the Fire that took over three-and-a-half hours and ended with four players fouling out. The Mystics have won a league-high 17 clutch games, defined as games that are within five points in the final five minutes of the fourth quarter and overtime.

Last year at this time, the team simply wanted to make it together through the season — the league’s first to feature 44 games.

Before the season Iriafen branded this year the “44 and more,” making it clear the postseason was the objective.

On Aug. 23, for the first time in three years, Washington clinched a playoff berth.

“We stayed in the moment, but we were also aspirational. We were like, ‘Hey, we can do a little bit more here,’” Johnson said. “I'm not saying we forecasted where we are right now, but I did know that and felt like we were going to be better.”
