entries.title: Democrats Brace for a Crypto PAC Cash Avalanche
entries.summary: After blocking the crypto industry’s preferred bill, Senate Democrats are pointing blame at Republicans to combat a potential $100 million onslaught.
entries.content:
After Senate Democrats blocked a bill to regulate cryptocurrency on the Senate floor last week, the industry’s major Super PAC network announced the first installment in what is expected to be a heavy wave of spending before the midterm elections.

Fairshake will spend $30 million on ads targeting former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio before November, and it expects to unleash additional spending in the “coming days and weeks,” Geoff Vetter, a Fairshake spokesman, told The Washington Sun.

Unlike in years past, though, Fairshake could distribute its $100 million in cash on hand much more heavily for Republicans, said a source familiar with the crypto industry who requested anonymity in order to discuss the political calculations.

“Elizabeth Warren forced her caucus to choose between consumer protection and pure politics,” the source said of Fairshake’s evaluation of who to support.

Crypto spending historically has been bipartisan, but every Senate Democrat voted to block the industry-backed CLARITY Act over concerns it allowed President Donald Trump and his family to profit from a number of crypto interests. Fairshake and other groups largely held off on spending while the bill was tied up in the chamber.

Now, Democrats like Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who have enjoyed good relationships with crypto groups, are walking a fine line as they try to preserve their standing with the industry.

Slotkin said she continues to speak with crypto groups about Democrats’ position on the industry. Those groups spent about $10 million supporting Slotkin in her 2024 race, a contest she won by only 0.3 percentage points.

“I think it’s important that we have regulation over crypto,” Slotkin said. “I just can’t sign onto a bill that gives permission, literally a handwritten permission slip, to the president of the United States to milk the American people and make money off of them.”

Slotkin’s talks come as Republicans who led CLARITY Act negotiations push for crypto groups to spend big against Democrats. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyoming) called the caucus’ blanket opposition to the bill “shameful.”

“I want them to spend it only on people who voted to proceed on CLARITY,” Lummis said of her hope for crypto groups. She added it would be a “huge mistake” for the industry to help Democrats who she said drew out negotiations, secured 126 amendments to the bill and still stalled it.

Some Democrats involved in those negotiations pushed back. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who voted with Republicans to advance the bill out of committee, pointed to Senate Republicans and the president for the bill’s failure.

“Republican leadership shut it down at the very last minute after it became clear that we were on a path to a successful vote,” Alsobrooks said in a statement. “I am proud of the progress we made, and I am determined to keep fighting to regulate this technology.”

Other Democrats said they aren’t discouraged by the threat of spending by the industry. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), the top Democrat on the Senate Banking committee, cast doubt on the idea that crypto groups were ever bipartisan to begin with.

“They should take [the bill failing] up with Donald Trump,” Warren said. “People across this country are sick of a handful of billionaires who think they can buy every election. The 2026 midterms will put that issue squarely on the table.”

The cryptocurrency industry has historically spent more to support GOP candidates –– Fairshake and its affiliates directed roughly $53 million to Republicans and $33 million to Democrats in 2024.

Brown, who lost his seat in 2024 after the crypto industry spent $40 million in his race, has already begun fundraising off of Fairshake’s spending announcement. Brown preceded Warren as the top Democrat on the banking panel and repeatedly criticized the industry as a sitting senator.

“Of course the special interests are panicking, they know Sherrod will fight the rigged system they're feasting on to stand up for working Ohioans,” Patrick Eisenhauer, Brown’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

The CLARITY Act did, though, see some opposition from Republicans. Voting with Democrats were Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Jerry Moran of Kansas, who largely cited the potential for impacts on small banks in their states.

Banking groups mounted a multi-million dollar lobbying blitz in August to push lawmakers, including many Republicans, to oppose the bill. Fairshake did not answer questions about whether it plans to spend money to defeat any Republican candidates this cycle.

The crypto source suggested that the industry believes the banking industry deserves a significant share of the blame for the CLARITY Act’s failure, and that some groups might not go all in against Democrats who could be in power next year.

“It was really the banks who made a decision to wage war over this issue on this bill," the source said. “They succeeded.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who defeated Brown in 2024 and has been a champion for crypto interests in the upper chamber, told The Sun he regretted that his conference couldn’t find unity on the bill.

But, Moreno added, supporting any Democratic candidates was “mistake one” for crypto groups. The unified Democratic opposition itself proves that the lobby should continue boosting Republicans ahead of November regardless of a few defections, he said.

“I’m a little disappointed with my three Republican colleagues that we didn't stick together,” Moreno said. “But look, it was 47 out of 47 Democrats. … They made it clear they wouldn’t even consider the bill.”

entries.title: Judge Orders the White House to Reinstate Access to Banned Outlets
entries.summary: The federal judge said the White House failed to back up its claims that the bans were needed for national security.
entries.content:
The Trump administration must temporarily restore access to MS NOW, CNN and Politico, a federal judge ruled early Thursday, nearly a week after President Donald Trump banned the outlets from the White House.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day restraining order and told the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” press credentials to journalists at the three outlets.

Trump said Friday that he was banning the outlets from the White House for reporting what he called “fake news.” The news organizations’ credentials were revoked on Saturday, and on Monday, the outlets filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, saying it had violated the journalists’ First Amendment rights.

The Justice Department argued in court Wednesday that the outlets’ reporting threatened national security, a new justification only used after the reporters’ access was revoked.

In his order, Kelly said that while security concerns are a “weighty interest,” the White House had failed to back up its assertions enough to justify the revocation — especially since mentions of “national security” came well after Trump’s initial post.

“Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote, adding that Trump’s primary focus was the “negativity” of the outlets’ reporting.

The government provided the court with a list of 13 stories that it said showed the outlets had jeopardized national security, but Kelly dismissed the declarations. He wrote that DOJ had filed nothing, classified or unclassified, that proved the stories cited risked national security. Kelly also downplayed statements filed by Defense Department officials in support of the ban, saying they have “no direct knowledge” of how White House reporting works.

Additional filings from the outlets show many of the reporters who wrote the stories in question “did not even hold hard passes,” Kelly, a Trump appointee, wrote. “In the remaining cases, Defendants afford no reason to believe that the reporter’s possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified.”

Dozens of media outlets from across the country publicly supported CNN, MS NOW and Politico through an amicus brief filed Wednesday, which argued Trump’s ban goes against the public interest and seeks to squash reporting the president may view as unfavorable.

“It is designed to have a chilling effect, with the hope that it discourages other outlets from publishing stories that they fear might provoke similar sanctions,” the brief said.

entries.title: How Progressive Powerhouses Put Their Endorsements to Work
entries.summary: The high-profile support can drive millions to candidates, but the timing makes a difference according to The Washington Sun’s analysis.
entries.content:
The older crowd may be on the outs for progressive Democrats, but if younger candidates want a campaign boost, the left wing’s old guard is where to turn first, a Washington Sun analysis of high-profile progressive endorsers finds.

It also found differing strategies in how the leading figures on the left decide when to formally bless aspirants to the U.S. House and Senate.

The analysis, which crunched data on endorsements from a number of leading figures on the left and subsequent donations from the endorsers’ networks in the current election cycle, found that through July 31 donors in Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders’ network contributed the most, followed by that of California Rep. Ro Khanna.

The Sanders imprimatur spurred his backers to dole out $9.1 million to 21 chosen candidates, for an average of more than $433,000, though the largest amount, $3.1 million went to the now-defunct Senate campaign of Maine’s Graham Platner. Khanna backed 15 congressional hopefuls, enticing his network to hand out an average of $227,000 to each campaign for a total of $3.4 million.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/jyU5U/1/Among high-profile Democrats like Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York) and Ilhan Omar (Michigan), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Massachusetts), Warren has generated the most endorsements and donations, picking 11 congressional candidates and helping generate nearly $2.7 million, an average of more than $242,000 per candidate.

Ocasio-Cortez and Omar have been more conservative in naming favorites. Before the analysis’ July 31 cut off, the New York representative anointed seven candidates, who received $1.8 million from her network for an average of over $257,000. Omar threw her support behind nine candidates who landed nearly $1.6 million, or just under $174,000 a piece.

The data also reveal differing strategies, with Sanders and Khanna taking a riskier endorse-often and endorse-early approach. Sanders’ backing came a median of 103 days before his choices’ primaries. Khanna’s median is 96. Warren’s median endorsement date is also a relatively long 82 days ahead of time.

In the case of Khanna, who harbors national ambitions but isn’t as well-known, the early aid can be helpful in raising his profile and building gratitude with up and coming progressives. He’s also backed numerous non-federal candidates. In Sanders’ case, it marks a shift, said Julian Mulvey, one of the architects of Sanders’ first presidential campaign.

He told The Washington Sun it once “took a long time” for candidates to earn the Vermont senator’s support, but “that’s changed” with this cycle’s slate of endorsements. He praised Sanders and Khanna for their aggressive strategies, which helped raise resources and the profiles of left-leaning candidates who have won primaries.

Sanders supporters like Mulvey acknowledged the risk of a shoot-fast-and-early endorsement strategy. Platner is the prime example, having soared to prominence with help from the millions Sanders’ donors forked over only to drop his bid in July amid allegations of sexual assault. Sanders endorsed Platner 283 days before his primary victory in June, and stood by the oysterman through numerous earlier flare ups before calling for Platner to quit after assault allegations became public.

Neither Ocasio-Cortez nor Omar ever endorsed Platner.

They wait until late, functioning more like closers in the final innings of primaries. Omar has endorsed candidates less than a month before their primaries — a median of 29 days. For Ocasio-Cortez, it’s just 20 days before the election.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/KIZxv/1/While the slower endorsements could be seen as a sort of Johnny-come-lately caution, it can also reflect the extraordinary — and often hostile — attention directed at the pair, especially at Ocasio-Cortez.

“I don’t think anyone can quite appreciate the astonishing level of scrutiny that falls on her, it is like no one else in the party,” Mulvey said about Ocasio-Cortez. “I give her a tremendous amount of leeway to figure this out, because no one else has to face that level or scrutiny. I don’t blame her at all for being very careful, very judicious.”

The later endorsements also have the effect of delivering a more concentrated stream of cash that comes in over a compressed time frame, perhaps when it’s needed most.

For instance, Sanders backed the Senate campaign of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan a full 474 days before the primary, and Khanna followed with an endorsement just a week later. Sanders supporters contributed nearly $2.1 million to El-Sayed after the endorsement, and Khanna’s network added just shy of $1 million.

Ocasio-Cortez endorsed El-Sayed just 33 days before his primary, and Omar threw her support behind the Michigan progressive 22 days before the election as the race was tightening. In the time after the endorsements, Ocasio-Cortez donors gave El-Sayed over $940,000 and Omar’s network contributed almost $735,000.

Another progressive strategist said the endorsements from Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and other leaders in the movement, no matter when they come through, are needed to capitalize on an environment that is “very amenable to progressive challengers.”

“Organizing is great, but even that requires money,” the strategist said. “Because progressive voters are extremely invested, a little money goes a lot further with them.”

The Sun determined the impacts of the endorsers by analyzing federal campaign finance records to identify donors who contributed to the progressive congressional leaders over several election cycles, then calculating how much those donors contributed in the 2026 midterm cycle to the campaigns that each lawmaker endorsed. Donors were matched using normalized names and ZIP codes. The analysis also examined the timing of endorsements, including how far ahead of an election they were made and when a leader’s donors began giving to endorsed candidates. The analysis supplemented Federal Election Commission data with ActBlue earmarked contribution data to capture small-dollar donations that do not always appear individually in a candidate’s FEC filings.

entries.title: Google Pulled Down a Trump-Linked Ad That Used AI
entries.summary: Google requires the disclosure of certain AI use in political ads.
entries.content:
Google this week removed a digital campaign ad from a super PAC aligned with Donald Trump because it failed to disclose the use of artificial intelligence, a violation of the platform’s rules, The Washington Sun has learned.

The ad, launched last week by No Going Back PAC, includes an AI-generated video of Johnny Garcia, the Democratic nominee in Texas’ 35th Congressional District, shaking his head in apparent frustration. The AI-generated clip was a few seconds long and embedded in a larger attack ad against Garcia.

Google’s political ad policy does not bar political advertisers from using AI to make it appear as if a person is doing or saying something they did not, but it does require advertisers to check a box to mark the content as AI generated.

Officials with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee reported the ad last Thursday. By Tuesday, it was no longer running online. Google, which owns YouTube, notified the DCCC that the ad had been removed from its platform “for a policy violation,” according to a screenshot the committee provided to The Sun.

“Carlos De La Cruz and his extremist Republican backers clearly have no issue lying to Texas voters,” DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus said in a statement, referring to the Republican nominee in the race.

The removal of the ad highlights the changing rules of political advertisements in the AI era, where rules over how to use video produced by the technology can differ from platform to platform. It also underscores how Republicans have thus far been more willing to use AI-produced ads than Democrats, pushing creative boundaries but risking voter backlash among those who consider the practice deceitful.

Representatives from No Going Back did not respond to a request for comment.

The race between Garcia and De La Cruz is rated as “likely Republican” by The Cook Political Report. But Democrats have said in recent weeks that they think the race is competitive despite the district’s Republican tilt, a sign of a strong environment for the party’s candidates that’s helping them compete in even deep-red areas.

A Spanish-language version of the ad remains in the super PAC’s Google political ad library. No Going Back PAC spent between $1,000 and $1,500 promoting the ad, which was shown between 50,000 and 60,000 times, according to Google ad library metrics.

There are no federal rules or regulations dictating the disclosure or use of artificial intelligence in political ads. No Going Back has spent more than $700,000 in the last eight days to run the spot over TV, according to AdImpact.

Representatives from Google did not respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Waymo Touts Its Crash Safety Data, But D.C. Won’t Release the Numbers
entries.summary: Autonomous vehicle companies — which could be permitted to operate in the District this fall — enjoy a blanket exemption from public records law.
entries.content:
Waymo released new crash safety data Thursday showing that across Atlanta, Austin, Los Angeles, Phoenix and San Francisco, its driverless vehicles were involved in 841 fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers.

But here in D.C. — where the autonomous vehicle company has been testing since April 2024 — if you request any crash data from D.C.’s Department of Transportation, you’ll come up short.

That’s because while the D.C. statute creating the city’s AV testing program required any “permit holder” to submit crash data to DDOT on a quarterly basis, it then provided those companies a blanket exemption from Freedom of Information Act requests for that information. DDOT is supposed to publish that data online itself, though it has not.

The statute’s opacity has raised concerns, as it means the D.C. council will soon vote on whether to permit driverless cars’ operation in the District without data on how many times AVs have crashed while testing here, and where and how those incidents happened. It’s debatable whether the statute, which DDOT cites when denying FOIA requests, even applies yet, as no AV company has yet been granted a permit to operate in the city.

“This data should be able to be reported,” Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who chairs D.C.’s transportation committee, told The Washington Sun. “In previous hearings, I've asked, ‘Well, have there been any crashes? What type of data are you reporting out?’ And DDOT had said that there have been no crashes, so we don't have a report to share.”

As of that July hearing, federal data shows that 14 AV-involved crashes had already happened in D.C., and a 15th happened that same month. AV companies are required to report to the federal government within a day of learning of a crash. Of the 15 crash incidents that a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration dashboard shows have happened to date since July 2021, six resulted in minor injuries — with one hospitalization — and four in property damage. The federal data is a start, but it lacks details including street addresses and exact dates. Multiple entries have the “narrative” section explaining what happened redacted entirely.

Eight of the incidents involved the Ford-backed, and since-folded, Argo AI; six involved Waymos and one involved a Beep, Inc. vehicle, a company that is currently inactive, according to DDOT.

Those numbers aren’t outlandish, especially when compared to citywide stats: Around 100,000 regular vehicle accidents happened in the same period, according to a Sun analysis of Open Data DC statistics, and there have been 236 traffic fatalities to date since 2021, according to D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department. It goes without saying that there are far more human-manned cars driving around D.C., but the data shows that the incidents DDOT is keeping under seal are relatively tame.

The Sun learned of the D.C. statute blocking a local release of those records when DDOT cited it to deny aJuly FOIA request for crash data from its AV testing program. Fritz Mulhauser, a D.C. attorney familiar with open records rules and a member of the board of the D.C. Open Government Coalition, doesn’t think the statute applies to the records requested, because technically the District doesn’t yet have “permit applicants and permit holders” subject to the exemption asAVs haven’t officially yet been rolled out here.

Allen doesn’t think the information should have been withheld even under the law as written.

“DDOT cannot deny the data that you were requesting because you didn't ask for any proprietary information,” Allen said. “And, big picture here, I do believe that being responsive to data requests is important, but I'd go beyond that. It shouldn't just have to be [that] someone's asking the question, there's a value in proactively reporting information.”

Allen said his bill legalizing the operation of driverless cars in the District would override the 2019 law, and has in place “robust” public reporting requirements on not just crashes but on response times, miles traveled with and without passengers and how many wheelchair-accessible rides were requested versus completed.

“It's not just about good oversight and accountability, I think it also builds trust in something that's new,” he said.

The Sun is appealing DDOT’s denial of that request with the mayor’s office, which expects to issue a final decision within the next few weeks. Allen said the information should be made publicly available in time for any further hearings or votes on AV operations.

“We're going to be following up with DDOT to make sure that we have a full accounting,” he said.

Mulhauser put it plainly.

“DDOT should release the crash reports from the test drives, and the council should ask why records that the federal government publishes are secret here,” he said.

entries.title: Reporters Turned Away From the White House Hours After Court Order
entries.summary: It’s not clear whether the incident represented “defiance of the court order or if it’s some kind of incompetence,” MS NOW reporter Laura Barrón-López said.
entries.content:
Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico all reported that they had been barred from entering the White House by the Secret Service Thursday morning despite a federal judge’s ruling hours earlier ordering the Trump administration to restore their access, which was revoked at the request of President Donald Trump.

The three outlets sued the Trump administration on Monday after Trump’s ban for reporting what he called “fake news.” After a hearing on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day restraining order, telling the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the journalists’ press credentials.

The outlets submitted a notice of the Trump administration’s noncompliance to the federal court in Washington and asked for an immediate hearing.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

CNN reported that the White House had denied access to reporter Betsy Klein, whose badge was confiscated on Saturday, and a photojournalist at about 6 a.m. Thursday. However, one CNN producer was allowed entry after 6 a.m. It is unclear why that person could access the building, CNN said.

The network added that it will continue to seek access during business hours.

Politico published a story just after 8 a.m. saying the Secret Service denied access to one of its reporters and confiscated their badge. MS NOW reporter Laura Barrón-López was also denied access, the network said.

Barrón-López recounted the morning’s events on air, saying that after her press badge failed to grant her access, the Secret Service agent told her it was “still being disabled.”

“It’s not clear based on the interaction that I had whether or not this is a defiance of the court order or if it’s some kind of incompetence or lag in the system where they have not updated our press badges,” Barrón-López said.

CNN, Politico and MS Now did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Trump administration argued in court filings that concerns about national security caused the ban and included in an exhibit a list of stories that prompted the action. A majority of the identified articles included reporting that was critical about the war in Iran and Trump’s White House ballroom project.

Kelly, a Trump appointee whom the president called out on social media ahead of the ruling, wrote in his order that while security concerns are a “weighty interest,” the White House did not provide sufficient evidence to justify the ban. 

“Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote, adding that Trump appeared to focus on the “negativity” of the outlets’ reporting.

The ban resulted in other television networks declining to participate in the White House pool, the group of journalists who travel with Trump daily to broadcast video and audio from his events, in a show of solidarity. 

Without the experience and infrastructure provided by the major TV networks, Trump’s press events have been marred by technical difficulties, including several appearances without audio. 

The White House subsequently announced its own livestream broadcast channel called “Trump TV,” which was unveiled the same day as the president first experienced audio difficulties due to the media blackout.

The ongoing drama also coincides with a lavish state visit from Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is scheduled to participate in a full slate of events at the White House Thursday.

entries.title: Navy Reveals Eight Service Members Aboard the USS Lincoln Attempted Suicide
entries.summary: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao maintains that the mental health resources provided on the ship “have been adequate to meet the spiritual and emotional needs of the crew.”
entries.content:
Eight personnel with the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide while serving as part of the ship’s record-breaking deployment, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao obtained by The Washington Sun.

Cao was responding to questions from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) about the conditions and well-being of sailors aboard the ship. The letter was first reported by CNN.

None of the personnel died, but Cao reported two attempted “man overboard” incidents had occurred. One sailor went overboard in August and was “quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter, treated by LINCOLN's medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care,” Cao wrote. The other sailor attempted to go overboard in March but was stopped by his shipmates.

Cao maintained that the mental health resources provided on the ship “have been adequate to meet the spiritual and emotional needs of the crew,” and said a comparative analysis of the Navy’s record for “mishap reporting shows no elevated mishap rates for the LINCOLN during its current deployment when compared to other carriers.”

The Lincoln remained deployed for more than 300 days before ending its assignment on Aug. 19, when the USS George Washington relieved the aircraft carrier. The Lincoln spent about seven months without a port stop aiding U.S. operations against Iran in the Arabian Sea, a record.

When the ship’s prolonged deployment began to make news this summer, President Donald Trump brushed the concerns aside, telling reporters in August that the deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

Cao carefully addressed the lengthy operation for the ship, saying the department makes “every effort to limit extensions, executing them only when critical national security requirements leave no other viable alternative.”

Reports emerged in early August of depleted food supplies and substandard hygiene aboard the ship after MS NOW spoke with families of some of the service members. At the time, the Navy pushed back on the reports, and though Cao addressed some of the concerns in his letter, dated Sept. 22, he appeared to downplay any negative speculation about living conditions.

“The ship has encountered no medical supply issues,” Cao said in response to a question about the medical care on board.

Photos have circulated of extremely small portions of food served on the ship this year, supporting family member’s accounts.

Reports also indicated that sailors had seen potentially contaminated water on the ship, and had to use broken toilets and moldy showers.

“Earlier in deployment, the ship experienced localized piping failures and temporary issues with its reverse osmosis desalination units due to high-ambient seawater temperatures and continuous operations,” Cao said, adding that the issue was fixed and “the potable water supply remains safe and tested daily.”

Gillibrand, who is on the Senate Armed Services Committee, called Trump and the Defense Department’s lack of effort to address issues during the Lincoln’s deployment “completely unacceptable.”

“What Trump and Secretary [Pete] Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a statement. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect.”

Cao confirmed in the letter that a “bipartisan Congressional Delegation is in the planning stages to embark the LINCOLN following the ship's return home.”

entries.title: The Senate Won’t Tackle Affordability Before the Midterms
entries.summary: The chamber will be in session next week but what they do after they wrap a college sports bill is unclear.
entries.content:
Gas and diesel prices are spiking due to the Iran war, making life hell for American farmers. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is making consumer goods more expensive for everyone. Mortgage rates topped 7%. Tech leaders are sounding the alarm about artificial intelligence and its risk to humanity.

The Republican-controlled Congress is focused on college sports.

More than 70 senators have backed the Protect College Sports Act, which would establish a unified federal framework for intercollegiate athletics, including standards for player compensation, transfers and eligibility.

Typically, a rare bipartisan piece of legislation is something people celebrate. But the Senate is using up weeks of floor time ahead of the midterms, resulting in complaints from even some of the bill’s supporters who aren’t happy about the chamber’s priorities right now.

“If you think moms and dads, when they lie down to sleep at night, are worried about whether the football coaches are happy, you need to back off the crank,” Sen. John Kennedy (R- Louisiana) told reporters this week. “We need to be dealing with bills to affect the cost of living. We haven't. We haven't done anything since the One Big Beautiful Bill.”

“We seem to be focused on issues many of you don't even care about,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) vented to his followers on X. “We're just not doing what we should be doing to deal with issues you care about.”

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) also urged his colleagues to stay in D.C. and work on safeguards around AI.

“The Republicans set the schedule, and they've demonstrated they are laser focused on things that people are not talking about,” Schatz said.

Republican leadership initially hoped to wrap up legislative business this week after clearing the college sports bill, but pressure from rank-and-file senators to do more to address high prices will keep the chamber in another week. Any real legislation to do things like regulate AI would have to wait until after the November election, though Trump has said he’s adamantly opposed to implementing guardrails.

It’s likely the college sports bill won’t get a vote until Monday at the earliest due to the Senate’s rules, but what they actually do after that is wrapped is unclear. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the chamber would likely not work on Friday, but they might take up a bill that aims to address rising costs due to data centers next week. Though even that wasn’t a sure thing.

“You know, [energy] ratepayer protections [legislation] is an option, there's another bill that a number of our members have an interest in. So at this point, we're kind of in that posture,” he told reporters. “You guys all know we've been here before this, where you kind of figure it out as we go. But part of anything around here, this time requires some level of cooperation or consent … and you know we're not seeing much out of the Democrats on that.”

Voter concerns about high prices have rattled Republicans in key battleground races across the country, with some calling on Trump to end the war in Iran and take actions to lower the record cost of diesel, which is hitting farmers hard across the Midwest.

“The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers,” Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate in Iowa, wrote on X.

Other Republicans are pushing for a vote in the Senate on long-stalled federal permitting legislation and a bipartisan bill passed overwhelmingly by the House that’s designed to shield consumers from costs associated with large data centers.

During his weekly press conference on Wednesday, Thune said he hoped to move both bills, but that doing so would depend on agreement from Democrats and the willingness of senators to stay in town another week.

“We can certainly try to tee it up,” Thune said of the data center bill. “It would take some cooperation from Democrats to get on it, but if we can get on it, I think it’s a worthwhile effort to try and get that bill passed.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said the Senate ought to focus on passing aid to farmers and bolstering the nation’s defense.

“The other things most people aren't going to run to the polls over,” Tillis said, referring to the college sports bill. “They're not just not leading major political rallies in North Carolina.”

Kennedy warned his party not to be dismissive about the cost of living and that it “doesn't do any good to tell [Americans] that it doesn't exist.”

“You can't look the American people in the eye and say, ‘Don't believe your lying checkbooks,’ he said. “Okay, and the cost-of-living increases is caused mostly by the Iran war, and we ought to be addressing it and the things we can do to address it. But I'm disappointed that we haven't even tried.”

entries.title: Trump’s FDA Nominee Sidesteps Senators’ Questions on Vaccines and Abortion
entries.summary: Heidi Overton, whose confirmation has an uncertain future, gave careful answers during her Senate confirmation hearing Thursday.
entries.content:
Heidi Overton studiously avoided sharing her personal views on vaccines, abortion medication and birth control Thursday, instead citing Food and Drug Administration policy on a gauntlet of questions from senators considering her to lead the agency.

The hearing was rife with potholes for Overton, President Donald Trump’s nominee for commissioner of the agency which regulates the nation’s drugs and is also central to hotly debated administration initiatives on abortion medication mifepristone, flavored vapes and vaccines.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, pressed Overton to say what she’d do if her bosses — Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — ordered her to undermine vaccines.

“I think the role of FDA commissioner if confirmed and what I would do is communicate and use my scientific training and clinical background to describe what is currently known,” Overton responded.

“And what is currently known is the vaccines approved by FDA have met the standards for safety and efficacy,” she added.

Overton, who stood near Trump in the Oval Office a few weeks ago as he said the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal,” did say “the MMR vaccine is safe and effective.”

Later in the hearing, when pressed by Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-New Hampshire), Overton wouldn’t say whether Trump was wrong to question the vaccine’s safety.

Cassidy, a doctor who has hounded Trump nominees on their beliefs about vaccines before ultimately voting for them, appeared unsatisfied by Overton’s responses. He pressed her to explain what role the president should play in determining vaccine safety.

Overton responded that policy priorities can be set by the president but said most individual product determinations are done by career staff with expertise, calling that "appropriate.”

Cassidy hasn’t said whether he plans to vote to confirm Overton.

Overton also wouldn’t say directly whether she believes mifepristone, a medication commonly used for abortions, is safe. FDA is reviewing the safety of the drug, which was approved with extra safety protocols decades ago by FDA.

“I know it has met the safety and efficacy standards according to FDA review,” Overton said in response to questions by Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington).

Murray also asked Overton whether she believes IUDs are abortifacients, a position held by some abortion opponents.

“If I’m confirmed as FDA commissioner I’ll be fully briefed on all their prior decisions and make determinations according to the standards of safety and efficacy,” Overton responded.

“I don’t think you answered the question,” Murray responded.

entries.title: Classified Estimates Show the NSA Is Paying Billions to Test AI Models
entries.summary: The price tag is significantly higher than previously known.
entries.content:
The National Security Agency told lawmakers that it is spending billions of dollars in taxpayer funds this year evaluating and testing advanced artificial intelligence models, according to two sources familiar with classified intelligence estimates.

The price tag — which is significantly greater than previously known — has led lawmakers to believe that a more comprehensive AI regulatory system could cost the government tens of billions of dollars per year, the sources said.

President Donald Trump has mostly resisted calls for greater federal oversight of AI, rejecting regulatory proposals from members of Congress and the frontier labs aimed at imposing new safeguards on the models. But after a string of high-profile hacking and security incidents, the NSA’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center began testing frontier models to identify potential national security vulnerabilities.

The high cost of those efforts is bringing new urgency to the debate about the government’s role in reviewing AI models designed by some of the most powerful and resourceful companies in the world. It also may intensify calls to have the frontier labs to shoulder the financial burden of reviewing the models, especially with spending set to only balloon as the technology grows more advanced.

Estimates of prior proposals to establish new federal AI regulatory oversight suggested a far lower price tag.

For instance, the Congressional Budget Office estimated the AI Security and Innovation Act, a bipartisan House proposal to establish a center on AI risks and "facilitate the mitigation of those risks," would cost roughly $20 million per year.

A separate bill in the House to establish a new reporting and tracking system for AI calls for $36 million in total over the next five years, the CBO reported.

Some tech leaders, like billionaire Elon Musk, have suggested that the frontier labs should review each other’s models prior to their release without government oversight. On Thursday, The Information reported that Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are jointly working on a plan to create their own AI safety-focused "standards body.”

But some AI safety experts have rejected this model as effectively allowing the firms to police themselves. One alternative is for the government to levy a tax on AI companies to run these safety operations — both to ensure independence and to ensure the financial burden of regulating AI does not fall primarily on the taxpayers. Anthropic and OpenAI have suggested that they want greater federal oversight and may be open to paying for it as well.

Currently, NSA’s AI testing efforts are being funded by classified portions of the federal national security budget, the two sources familiar said. The exact dollar amount the government has spent so far is not clear.

The Pentagon declined to comment on what the NSA is spending on AI.

“For security reasons, the Department does not discuss the technical architecture or resource allocation for its AI tools,” a spokesperson for the Defense Department said.

The Defense Department’s annual budget is close to $1 trillion. Some budgetary funds already allocated to the military could be shifted into AI-related spending, reducing the potential price tag.

One source said the biggest AI-related cost to the NSA thus far has been the extra computing power: the processing on chips necessary to run and test the AI models. Purchasing computing power has become incredibly expensive worldwide amid a surge in demand accompanied by insufficient production of chips. For instance, Anthropic has lined up computing deals that could cost as much as $517 billion, according to The Information.

Another big expense is in hiring personnel. Some top AI engineers have been offered salaries in the hundreds of millions of dollars, far outpacing what the government could match. NSA is widely regarded as having the deepest roster of technical experts within the government and still may not be able to compete with the giant pay packages thrown around by the frontier labs.

“Having in-house AI evaluation capability I think is extremely important and necessary. But it is genuinely expensive,” said Nathan Calvin, general counsel at Encode, an AI advocacy organization. “You’re competing in bidding with some of the most price-insensitive customers.”

Some experts have pushed for lawmakers to swiftly move to strengthen third-party audits of the models. Nat Purser, director of U.S. Policy at the AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute, said that while “people often underestimate how much computing power it can take to rigorously test advanced AI systems,” the government should make the investments necessary. Purser also said the AI companies could foot the bill if taxpayers are paying large sums to evaluate the models.

“If we want the government to be equipped to assess these systems, we need to fund the computing resources and expertise that requires,” Purser said. “I think of these tests as public goods, but there are reasonable questions about if taxpayers should foot the bill. An assessment on frontier developers could be required to help fund these independent audits, including the necessary computing resources.”

entries.title: Democrats Are Fighting Over How Bosses Should Treat Them After an Explosive Mary Peltola Report
entries.summary: Former staffers for the Alaska Senate candidate described fits of anger and use of slurs to The New York Times. Now Democrats are asking: Do we have to put up with that?
entries.content:
A news report about Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s anger toward staff members has Democrats asking themselves: Should we tolerate that?

Democrats piled on against anyone who thinks her behavior crossed a line, following a New York Times report detailing allegations from Peltola’s former staffers of angry outbursts in her time as a member of the House and during her current Senate campaign.

Instead, just six weeks from Election Day, many Democrats are arguing that Peltola’s staffers were too sensitive.

“The timing of this story and the weakness of the claims just kind of underscores the fact that these people don’t care about winning when the stakes are really high!” a veteran Democratic operative told The Washington Sun. “We’re in the ‘just win baby’ window of campaigning.

Like if she had pulled a gun on someone, that would hopefully merit a different response. But this is just like … get over yourself.”

The story has consumed the Democratic Party in a crucial stretch of campaign season. Peltola is running against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in one of the country’s most competitive races, which is expected to play a key role in deciding the Senate majority.

Several veterans of Democratic campaigns pointed out online that the staffers who spoke to The New York Times are emblematic of a broader culture problem with their party. They argue that Democratic staffers are too sensitive and demand working conditions not suited for the tense, fast-paced culture of a high-stakes campaign.

“Democrats right now are trying to shake this image of being like the soft, collegial academics,” said Yemisi Egbewole, a senior fellow at Third Way and former Biden administration staffer. “It's all this conversation about the working class, searching for grittier, tougher candidates, and meanwhile, the staffer class remains just the very soft academics that we make fun of here.”

The Times story describes an instance in 2024 in which Peltola allegedly shoved a staff member because she couldn’t find a memo for a meeting. The sources also described her use of the slur “faggot” to the outlet, which also reported a screenshot of a text Peltola sent referring to someone as a “retard.” In another text described by the outlet, she said of someone else: “I hope she dies of a botched abortion.”

The pattern of behavior also reportedly veered into the odd: Some of the staffers said she asked them to feed her daughter’s pet chameleon. More recently, she reportedly grew frustrated that the campaign did not have enough large campaign signs. “OUR SIGN GAME IS FUCKED” she said in texts seen by the outlet.

The campaign denied to the Times that Peltola’s actions amounted to a pattern of abusive behavior and denied her use of the homophobic slur. Her team also described the incident of physical contact with the staffer as a bump, rather than a shove, while the then-lawmaker was distracted. The campaign acknowledged to the newspaper that Peltola sometimes struggled to manage her grief after her mother and husband died in the span of a few months in 2023.

Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

Democrats also said there is a double standard, for both women and Democrats.

“I simply will not be lectured to about decorum from the folks supporting Ken Paxton, Bo French, Max Miller, Mike Collins, and Brandon Herrera,” Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, said on X.

Female politicians are often subject to harsher scrutiny, some Democrats argued.

“I have definitely heard stories of male members of both houses being total nightmares but apparently no reporter has,” Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress and a veteran of presidential campaigns, wrote on X. “Because somehow we get these stories about women leaders exclusively.”

Other Democrats acknowledged that Peltola’s behavior was inappropriate, even if they believed the former staffers’ handling of it was, too.

“Two things can be true: (1) It's not great nor effective when bosses (in any context) yell at or are otherwise shitty to their employees. AND: (2) Going to the NYT to complain about that behavior is almost never the correct response & will do more harm than good,” Amanda Litman, president of Run for Something, a progressive organization that recruits young candidates, wrote on X.

The main lesson for the party, many Democrats argued, is that in a race this competitive, campaign staff should do whatever it takes to get the candidate into office. This is not the first time Democrats have vented this type of frustration about griping — a similar conversation took hold when the Democratic National Committee ordered its staff to return to in-person work.

“There’s something deeply broken in the culture of Democratic Party staffing that people would think it is unreasonable to be asked to feed your boss’s pet while she does a job that involves commuting back and forth to Alaska,” wrote Matthew Yglesias, a Democratic commentator.

entries.title: Xi Kicks Off White House Visit With a Veiled Shot About Doing Business in the U.S.
entries.summary: “China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies. … We hope that Chinese companies are treated fairly,” he said.
entries.content:
President Xi Jinping of China opened his time at the White House with a subtle shot at America’s hesitancy to welcome Chinese businesses.

“China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there,” Xi said Thursday in translated remarks, as protesters chanted outside the White House grounds. “We hope that Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States.”

Xi and President Donald Trump are expected to speak about multiple issues involving Chinese business interests in the American market, including questions about artificial intelligence competition and potentially allowing Chinese automakers to establish factories in America.

Trump said in early September that he would support the idea of Chinese cars being built in the U.S.

“If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” Trump told Fox News at the time, adding that he’d want them to hire American workers. “Japan does it, but they hire our people.”

U.S. automakers are worried about the implications of a possible agreement. A coalition of industry groups wrote a letter to Trump ahead of the summit emphasizing that China’s exclusion from the U.S. market is essential to American automakers’ success. The letter also pointed to the security threats of allowing vehicles with Chinese technology to be bought and used in America.

National security concerns about Chinese technology and business have existed for years. The federal government has largely established laws and practices to prevent certain technology, such as Chinese-manufactured cellphones, from reaching the U.S. market, fearing it would compromise security.

Earlier this year, ByteDance, the Chinese company that owned TikTok, was forced to separate U.S. operations after Congress passed a bill requiring new ownership of the app if it was to continue operating in America.

Xi also broached AI, which is expected to be a major topic between the delegations this week.

“We have both the capability and the responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said.

Before Xi’s arrival, Trump reiterated his preference for continued innovation, even as some in the industry have voiced concerns about regulation being needed after instances of rogue AI agents.

“Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Thursday morning. “That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!”

After the initial remarks, Trump led Xi to the Rose Garden for a military review. The U.S. Army Old Guard Fife and Drum Corps and the U.S. Marine Corps Silent Drill Platoon demonstrated ceremonial maneuvers before the Chinese leader.

A flyover — the second that Xi has experienced since arriving — comprising a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 stealth fighters punctuated the ceremony, as the two leaders left the pageantry behind and reentered the West Wing to begin closed-door meetings.

entries.title: Kyrsten Sinema’s Ex-Bodyguard Is Accused of a $200K Art-Destroying Rampage at Her Home
entries.summary: The incident is the latest fallout surrounding Sinema’s relationship with her ex-bodyguard, who was married while working on her security detail.
entries.content:
Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s home was damaged in a wild, art-destroying rampage late last month by a former member of her security detail and ex-lover, according to court records.

The records, first reported by AZFamily, show 39-year-old Matthew Ammel entered Sinema’s Arizona home while she was out of town and allegedly destroyed paintings, bottles of alcohol and other property, causing what investigators estimated to be more than $200,000 in damage. The paintings alone were valued at $123,015, according to the probable cause statement.

Sinema told deputies that Ammel demanded she post a video to her X account and threatened to destroy one of her paintings “every 10 minutes” until she did, according to local media reports. When she refused, investigators say, Ammel removed about 22 paintings from the walls and threw them into the home’s swimming pool. One more painting was found near the home’s entrance with spray paint on it, AZFamily reported.

Ammel was taken into custody last week and faces a Class 4 felony criminal-damage charge. He was subsequently released with an electronic monitor and is due back in court for a preliminary hearing scheduled for next month.

Sinema provided investigators with text messages, recordings and surveillance footage, according to the court documents. Deputies said they reviewed the footage and were able to identify Ammel as the person damaging the property.

The incident is the latest development in the legal fallout surrounding Sinema’s relationship with Ammel, who was married while he was working on her security detail.

Ammel’s ex-wife, Heather Ammel, sued Sinema under North Carolina’s “homewrecker” law. The lawsuit accuses Sinema of contributing to the breakdown of the Ammels’ marriage and seeks financial damages from the former senator.

Sinema has acknowledged having a sexual relationship with Matthew Ammel. In a deposition taken in July, she said the relationship became sexual on May 27, 2024, during a trip to Napa Valley, California. She also testified that they later had sexual encounters in New York, Washington, Colorado and Arizona, but not in North Carolina.

Sinema, who left the Democratic Party in 2022 to become an independent, declined to seek reelection in 2024 and left the Senate in January 2025. She now works in the private sector.

entries.title: Commanders Dismiss Criticism They Abandoned Jayden Daniels After Injury
entries.summary: “It's just the opposite of that,” said coach Dan Quinn. “They were gutted. They love this guy.”
entries.content:
The Commanders are pushing back against the narrative that the team abandoned quarterback Jayden Daniels on the field after he dislocated his elbow in Sunday’s loss to the Cowboys.

Daniels went down on the final play of the first half after tripping over offensive lineman Chris Paul and planting his hand on the ground while trying to catch his fall. A brief clip of the Fox broadcast showed Commanders players walking by Daniels as the team’s medical staff attended to him.

The clip received little fanfare at the time, but drew comparisons after Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart injured his knee against the Rams on Monday night and had the whole team around him shortly after.

“It's bullshit what people are saying,” Commanders left tackle Brandon Coleman told reporters Wednesday. “Jay's our guy and he's been our guy.”

Commanders coach Dan Quinn clarified that players wanted to stay and support Daniels, but because the play happened right before halftime, they had to head to the locker room or risk losing time for their break.

“When the half is over, the referees are saying, 'Man, I can't delay the half. They can't stay on the field.' The players were like, 'No, we want to stay,’” Quinn said. “So it's just the opposite of that. They were gutted. They love this guy. So halftime was hard and emotional in that space.”

Multiple players stood around Daniels in the immediate aftermath of his injury before heading to the locker room. Players said Wednesday that both Quinn and officials told players to clear the sideline after lingering in support of Daniels.

“We stayed on the field, and once they got it situated and did what they had to do we checked on him,” Coleman said. “Dan told most [players] to go into the locker room. But it's tough to go in when you see something like that. You see the whole starting line out there, a bunch of receivers, some defensive guys.”

Daniels is out for Sunday’s game against the Seahawks and is currently seeking other opinions on his elbow, according to Quinn. Backup Marcus Mariota will start in his place.

entries.title: Chinese Press Corps Scuffles With U.S. Media and Secret Service
entries.summary: One Chinese journalist shoved a U.S. photographer in the press briefing room, according to videos posted online.
entries.content:
Members of the Chinese press corps in Washington for a state visit by the country’s president, Xi Jinping, got into several altercations with U.S.-based journalists and the Secret Service while covering President Donald Trump’s summit with Xi on Thursday, according to videos posted to social media.

The Washington Sun observed members of the Chinese press arguing loudly with White House aides in order to get a better position during a military review in the Rose Garden, which was part of the Thursday summit’s arrival ceremony.

The back-and-forth came atop an already drama-filled day in the White House press corps, as CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters fought to secure reentry to the grounds even after a federal judge temporarily struck down a ban that was originally put in place by Trump.

Chaos appeared to erupt in videos posted online as Chinese and U.S. media members jockeyed for a spot ahead of Xi’s arrival. One member of the U.S. press can be heard exclaiming, “You’re stepping on my feet,” in a video posted to X on Thursday by The Telegraph’s chief Washington correspondent, Connor Stringer.

The Secret Service reportedly became involved after an altercation regarding the placement of U.S. press and official Chinese state-run media on the White House South Lawn. Secret Service and White House officials threatened to remove one Chinese official “for interfering with shots and official WH cams,” according to Washington Examiner White House correspondent Christian Datoc’s account of the incident.

Following the altercations at the arrival ceremony, shouts rang out in the White House briefing room when a Chinese photographer reportedly shoved a female American reporter while rushing to the bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi in the Oval Office, according to a video and information posted to X by Iris Tao, the White House correspondent for NTD News, a news outlet founded by Chinese Americans that fled communism.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth appeared to react to a disruption created by the visiting press corps during remarks given by Trump and Xi in the Grand Foyer of the White House, according to Mary Margaret Olohan, the White House correspondent for the Daily Wire.

The White House, the U.S. Secret Service and the White House Correspondents’ Association did not respond to requests for comment on the incidents.

Despite the apparent distractions, Trump complimented the Chinese media, telling Xi that he admired Chinese reporters for their friendliness and deference — quipping that they have to ask Xi before they speak.

China has severely limited press freedoms, and many of the country’s reporters work for state-run media outlets. Trump’s ban on three outlets from entering White House grounds also forced some members of the U.S. press to adjust some of their coverage of the summit, after the network TV pool suspended its coverage in solidarity.

Taylor Rogers, a White House deputy press secretary, dismissed concerns about the optics of Trump’s media ban ahead of the U.S.-China summit.

“There is no comparison,” Rogers said in an interview with Spectrum News, speaking about China and U.S. press freedoms. “This is the most transparent president that our country has ever seen.”

This is not the first time incidents between U.S. officials and the Chinese press have been reported. Chinese reporters knocked down and trampled a White House aide during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, the New York Post reported.

During then-first lady Michelle Obama’s visit to Beijing in 2014, members of the Chinese media pushed forward, separating her from her daughters, while members of the U.S. media were also physically pushed during the trip, according to The Washington Post.

entries.title: A Watchdog Says ICE Wasted Millions in Its Detention Expansion
entries.summary: The agency had no strategic plan as it bought warehouses to turn into migrant detention centers, a report says. It still doesn’t.
entries.content:
The Trump administration wasted millions of taxpayer dollars in its immigration detention expansion efforts because it didn’t have a strategic plan, a new watchdog report found.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement spent more than $20 million it can’t recuperate to turn warehouses into detention centers, an initiative the agency has since scaled back, the Government Accountability Office found.

“It is critical that the agency uses these taxpayer dollars efficiently and effectively,” the report published Thursday says. “In the absence of a comprehensive strategic plan to guide detention expansion, ICE has wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments.”

After spending $1.07 billion on purchasing 11 warehouses across the country in the first four months of 2026, ICE plans to sell all but four, the GAO report says. But it has also spent $7.7 million on costs like zoning and nearly $13 million on utilities, security and other services for the warehouses.

The agency could lose even more money if it sells the warehouses for less than $707 million, after paying millions more than previous buyers and appraisal values.

The Department of Homeland Security inspector general is also auditing warehouse purchasing plans that generated bipartisan backlash in Congress. The plan fell to the wayside once Markwayne Mullin became Homeland Security secretary.

Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) was one of the lawmakers who requested the report.

“Remember when Donald Trump promised to get rid of ‘waste, fraud, and abuse’ in Washington?” Durbin said in a social media post. “Well, GAO continues to uncover incompetence and waste at the highest levels of ICE. Americans are outraged at ill-conceived immigration detention projects, and it’s time to hold DHS and ICE responsible.”

The Trump administration is moving ahead with other initiatives to ramp up its detention space without a strategic plan, the GAO report says. The average daily population was more than 67,000 at the end of July, according to ICE data cited in the report. The number of authorized detention centers has roughly doubled, according to the report.

The GAO report comes as ICE has signed five construction contracts worth up to $7.3 billion in Arizona, California, Florida, New York and Texas, according to watchdog group Project Salt Box.

David Schmitt, DHS’ director of the Departmental Audit Liaison Office, wrote in a Sept. 15 letter to GAO that the department would come up with a plan by Aug. 31.

“Securing the nation’s borders and safeguarding the integrity of the immigration system is ICE’s primary focus, and ICE plans to continue to meet the growing demand for bedspace by streamlining the detention and removal processes and focusing on non-traditional facilities built specifically to support ICE’s needs,” Schmitt wrote.

GAO criticized that timeline. “Given ICE’s unprecedented multi-year detention funding and the potential for continued waste of taxpayer dollars, more timely completion may be warranted,” the report says.

The report states that ICE’s recent purchases of existing detention centers could also result in waste. In July and August, ICE purchased four facilities in California, Minnesota and Kansas for $2.2 billion from private prison giant CoreCivic.

“While officials told us that they considered risks, such as environmental liabilities and site history for the facilities they identified for potential purchase, ICE has not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities,” the report states.

entries.title: Trump Administration Asks SCOTUS to Let It Restart Its Third-Country Deportation Push
entries.summary: The administration wants to continue quick deportations to countries where immigrants have no ties.
entries.content:
By Lindsay Whitehurst

President Donald Trump's administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to again clear the way for continued quick deportations of immigrants to third countries where they have no ties.

The government asked for an immediate halt to lower court orders finding that people must have the chance to object before the U.S. government deports them to countries other than their homelands.

The justices previously allowed the deportation flights to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year. Since then, an appeals court has upheld a Boston-based judge’s final ruling that migrants must have a meaningful chance to argue a third-country deportation would put them in danger of persecution or torture.

The ruling didn’t prohibit those deportations outright but it lengthens the process. The government argues it has already led to the cancellation of a flight carrying 70 people with criminal convictions to three different countries.

“The government has been able to remove thousands of aliens to third countries in recent months, and thousands more are eligible for such removal,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

Trump's Republican administration has said that it sends people to third countries when it is unable to quickly return them to their homelands. Those third-country governments provide assurances that people won’t be persecuted or tortured, attorneys said.

The lower courts' legal requirements would mean cascading delays and could force the reworking of agreements with foreign countries, attorneys wrote.

James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security's general counsel, said Wednesday on X that 25,000 people in the U.S. illegally have been deported to third countries, calling those deportations “an essential public safety tool.”

The vast majority of the deportees have been sent to Mexico, but under a series of often-secret agreements, the administration has deported thousands of others to more than two dozen countries, from Liberia to Guyana.

Some have found themselves in countries they’d never heard of before their arrivals. Some also face serious safety risks, and are left with little choice except to return to the home countries they were fleeing.

This month, lawyers for two men deported to Equatorial Guinea said they were beaten and held at gunpoint in a hotel-turned-detention center by police who covered their heads with bags.

In his tweet, Percival included a video of Taylor Swift smiling and pointing to her wedding ring as she celebrated a touchdown by her husband, the football player Travis Kelce.

“How my wife looks at me when I tell her we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations,” Percival wrote.

The case comes amid a sweeping immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which has pledged to deport millions of people who are living in the United States illegally.

entries.title: Tom Tiffany’s Campaign Bars a Reporter From Entering Campaign Event
entries.summary: The Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate's team said the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporter had received prior notice that she could not cover the lawmaker’s roundtable.
entries.content:
Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany’s team blocked a Milwaukee news publication’s reporters from entering an event over what a campaign staffer reportedly called unfair coverage, according to the outlet and videos posted on social media.

The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel said in its coverage that Tiffany staffer Eric Brooks barred investigative journalist Mary Spicuzza from entering despite assurances from the Republican gubernatorial nominee earlier this week that reporters would be able to cover his campaign.

The Tiffany campaign said in a statement that Spicuzza had received notice on Wednesday that she would not be permitted to attend the lawmaker’s roundtable with military veterans. The campaign allowed a Journal Sentinel photojournalist to attend.

The team appeared to specifically take issue with the publication’s coverage of Tiffany’s opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who became the Democratic nominee after an upset win during August’s primary election. The two are locked in a tight race ahead of Election Day.

“We expect journalists to be balanced, and when you write multiple negative headlines about our campaign and not a single negative headline about David Crowley, as Mary Spicuzza has done, that is not balanced reporting,” the campaign’s statement read.

In a video posted to social media, a campaign staffer stood in a doorway to prevent Spicuzza from entering the event. As the reporter asked questions about her access, the staffer could be heard telling Spicuzza the campaign wanted her to “cover the race fairly.”

Journal Sentinel Executive Editor Greg Borowski defended the publication’s reporters in a statement Thursday.

"When our reporters cover campaigns and attend political events, they are there on behalf of the public,” Borowski said. “Blocking them blocks the public from vital information. Our aim is to help voters understand the candidates, their backgrounds and their positions. We will continue to pursue fair and unbiased coverage, despite campaigns creating unnecessary hurdles."

The incident occurred days after President Donald Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from entering the White House, a decision that sparked additional concerns about press freedoms and access. A federal judge ordered the White House to temporarily restore access on Thursday, and reporters were able to enter the grounds after an initial delay.

entries.title: California Supreme Court Orders Riverside County Sheriff to Return 650,000 Seized Ballots
entries.summary: The court said it was "unlawful" for the sheriff to have seized the ballots from a 2025 special election.
entries.content:
By Olga R. Rodriguez

SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A Republican California sheriff must return more than a half-million ballots he seized for an investigation into unfounded voting improprieties in a special election last year, the state Supreme Court ruled Thursday.

Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco in February seized approximately 650,000 ballots from a November 2025 special election on statewide congressional redistricting favorable to Democrats and pushed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. The measure easily passed statewide, and won in Bianco's county by roughly 80,000 votes.

The court called the ballots’ seizure “unlawful,” saying California law requires voted ballots to remain in the custody and control of election officials, even during a criminal investigation. Bianco must also “refrain from further handling of the ballots except as necessary to comply with our order,” the court said in an unanimous decision. Bianco did not immediately comment on the ruling.

“If election misconduct is suspected, the Elections Code provides several mechanisms for law enforcement to review and examine ballots without compromising their integrity,” the court wrote.

Bianco’s ballot investigation came as President Donald Trump has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 election, citing unsubstantiated instances of fraud. His administration in January seized ballots and other documents from an election office in Georgia. Some Republicans have mirrored Trump’s rhetoric on voting in their states.

Election officials and civil rights groups have been following the Bianco case carefully as they brace for the possibility that Trump or his allies may try to seize ballots in November.

Bianco said he confiscated the election materials as part of a criminal investigation after receiving a complaint from a local citizens group that the count was off. Local election officials had previously said the complaint was unfounded. Bianco, was running for governor at the time, but he did not make it through the primary.

Democratic Attorney General Rob Bonta immediately launched a legal challenge, arguing the sheriff had no authority over election materials and warning the seizure was designed to sow distrust in elections. He ordered Bianco to return the ballots, but Bianco did not.

“The Court has now made clear that this kind of defiance cannot stand, that the Attorney General has the authority to intervene when sheriffs take improper action, and that voted ballots belong in the custody of elections officials,” Bonta said Thursday.

The University of California, Los Angeles Voting Rights Project also sued the sheriff and the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on behalf of several Riverside County voters. The state Supreme Court last month heard arguments in both cases.

The Court also found that a search warrant does not override the state's electoral law.

“The Court’s decision reaffirms a basic principle that in California, the Election Code applies to everyone, including law enforcement,” said Chad Dunn, legal director and co-founder of the UCLA Voting Rights Project. “These are the voters’ ballots. They must be protected through the processes the Legislature has established. This ruling provides important clarity for election officials, law enforcement, and voters across California.”

Newsom on Saturday signed a bill that would prevent anyone from seizing ballots, as Bianco did.

Bianco began recounting the vote shortly after seizing the ballots using sheriff’s officials under the supervision of a special master appointed by a court but suspended it days later, citing mounting legal challenges from the state attorney general and the voting rights group. But he has not returned the ballots.

Bradley Hertz, who represented Bianco before the court, argued the sheriff had a legal duty to open a criminal investigation after receiving a complaint and he followed the penal code to carry out that investigation, first issuing search warrants in February.

Hertz said Bianco has not returned the ballots to the Riverside County Registrar of Voters because those ballots are “evidence.”

At the time of the ballots’ seizure, Bianco was one of two prominent Republicans running for governor in a crowded June primary. He did not advance to the general election and later announced plans to run for reelection as sheriff in 2028.

Xavier Becerra, a former state attorney general and Democrat running for governor, is part of the UCLA lawsuit to halt Bianco’s efforts.
