entries.title: Netanyahu, at the U.N., Calls Accusations of Genocide in Gaza the 'Biggest Lie of the Century'
entries.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said no Palestinian state will be established while he is Israel’s leader.
entries.content:
By Sam Metz

Allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza are not only false but “the biggest lie of the century,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told world leaders Thursday in a defiant speech that asserted his nation’s right to wage war against Iran — and was not heard by scores of delegates who trooped out before he started speaking.

Netanyahu, his voice rising in emphasis, said attacking Iran “was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make” and denounced as “moral cowards” a mass of delegates who walked out of the U.N. General Assembly when he took the podium to speak.

“In defending itself, Israel is also also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said. “In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes.”

When Netanyahu walked to the rostrum, a mix of cheers, boos and mass walkouts erupted. Scores of delegates marched out and a majority of visible seats sat empty afterward. “Order in the hall, please,” General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said repeatedly.

“If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now,” Netanyahu said.

His remarks — which at times sounded like a stump speech as Israel gears up for elections — came after a week filled with speeches by world leaders accusing Israel of genocide and war crimes in Gaza.''

The Palestinian Mission to the U.N. said in a message to many of the 193 U.N. member nations to bring as many staff as possible to the assembly hall and “collectively walk out of the assembly” once the Israeli prime minister is announced.

“This will send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end,” the message said.

Israel rejects allegations that it committed genocide and war crimes and is illegally occupying Palestinian territory. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government insists they are legal.

Netanyahu, who is prone to using visual aids during his General Assembly speeches, at one point held up a pager while reminding the audience of Sept. 17, 2024, when Israel remotely detonated thousands of pagers that had been distributed to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. The pager attack wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children.

He reminded the assembly of the scale of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people. “This is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours,” he said, or 16 times the death count on the 9/11 attacks that left nearly 3,000 people dead in New York.

Netanyahu thanked U.S. President Donald Trump for taking decisive action against Iran, and he insisted Israel would prevail: “We will continue to win because we have no other choice.”

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas also addressed the U.N. General Assembly earlier Thursday, delivering prerecorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.

The 90-year-old leader's popularity at home and relevance abroad have both waned. But in his remarks, Abbas made clear he did not intend to quietly accept being sidelined.

“We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. And we will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf,” Abbas said.

Though world leaders have repeatedly invoked the plight of Palestinians in speeches throughout the week, Abbas urged the international community to take more tangible action against Israel.

"How long will some countries continue to remain silent about Israel, or continue supplying it with weapons that it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the enormous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank," Abbas said. “What, then, is the international community waiting for before it acts to protect the Palestinian people?”

In past years, Netanyahu has used his General Assembly speech to both denounce the United Nations as biased and make Israel's case to world leaders. His address — scheduled for prime time in Israel — is the cornerstone of an abbreviated trip to the United States unfolding under the shadow of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling him a “war criminal” and pushing for his arrest.

Mamdani has acknowledged that New York does not have the authority to execute an International Criminal Court warrant but urged federal authorities to do so.

Israel has grown increasingly isolated throughout the war in Gaza. The war began on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked Israel, killing around 1,200 people and kidnapping 251. At least 73,922 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's subsequent offensive, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, part of the Hamas-run government whose numbers are generally considered reliable by the international community.

A ceasefire agreed to by Israel and Hamas last October halted the heaviest of the fighting and led to the release of the remaining hostages yet further steps have since stalled. Israel maintains control of most of Gaza and continues to carry out airstrikes on Palestinians near military-held zones. Hamas not disarmed or relinquished power and there has been no progress toward reconstruction in the mostly destroyed territory.

Netanyahu has said no Palestinian state will be established while he is Israel’s leader and has argued that the Palestinian Authority is not a partner for peace.

Netanyahu dismissed incidents of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents” throwing stones, chopping down olive trees and lighting fires.

“I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism,” the prime minister said before accusing foreign leaders and the international press of distorting the scale of violence in the West Bank.

Netanyahu’s government is dominated by settlers and their allies, including the Cabinet minister who oversees the police. There have been few arrests of settlers involved in attacks on Palestinians.

Israel captured the West Bank and east Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The Palestinians and much of the international community view the settlements as illegal and as an obstacle to creating a viable, contiguous Palestinian state.

Associated Press reporters Jennifer Peltz and Edith M. Lederer contributed.

entries.title: Survivor Wounded in Trump’s 2024 Assassination Attempt Has Died
entries.summary: Jim Copenhaver had sought damages for his injuries, arguing the Justice Department failed to prevent the shooting at a Trump rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.
entries.content:
Jim Copenhaver, who was seriously wounded during the 2024 assassination attempt on President Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died, House Republicans announced Thursday. He was 76.

“Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance,” House Republicans said in a statement. “We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time.”

The announcement did not specify a cause of death or say when Copenhaver died. Whether his injuries from the shooting contributed to his death was not immediately clear.

Copenhaver was shot twice by Thomas Crooks during the July 13, 2024, attack, suffering injuries to his arm and abdomen that left him with nerve damage, according to CBS Pittsburgh.

Trump, then the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, was struck in the ear. A Secret Service sniper killed Crooks, who had opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another rallygoer, Corey Comperatore, was killed during the shootout.

Despite surviving the shooting, Copenhaver suffered long-term health effects from his injuries.

Along with fellow rally attendee David Dutch, Copenhaver sued the Justice Department for compensatory damages in June, arguing his life-altering injuries were a direct result of "100% negligence" by the U.S. Secret Service and the Department of Homeland Security.

The lawsuits claimed that the government was liable due to a cascade of alleged security failures, including a lack of communication, missed warning signs and a failure to secure the rooftop where Crooks opened fire.

The lawsuit remains pending in Pennsylvania federal court.

entries.title: Gary Peters’ Last Act: One More Push for the Pentagon to Clean Up PFAS
entries.summary: The Michigan Democrat is introducing a bipartisan bill compelling the Defense Department to act, in a fight he knows will outlast him in Congress.
entries.content:
Sen. Gary Peters convened the Senate’s first hearing on PFAS contamination in 2018 and brought attention to Oscoda, Michigan, where residents had spent years pressing for action to clean up the “forever chemicals” contaminating the former Wurtsmith Air Force Base. He asked what the federal government could do to identify the contamination, protect residents and speed the cleanup.

Eight years later, Peters is preparing to leave the Senate and Wurtsmith is still on the Pentagon’s long list of U.S. military installations with delayed investigations into PFAS contamination. So are 10 other Michigan sites, according to Peters’ office. At Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center and Selfridge Air National Guard Base, projected dates for completing the investigation and study phase have slipped by 26 years.

Now the Michigan Democrat is introducing one last piece of legislation to force progress at the Pentagon, the PFAS RAPID Response Act. Within two years of the bill becoming law, the Defense Department would have to initiate interim actions at at least 100 of the 351 installations with delayed investigation schedules. It also requires a congressional briefing within 30 days of becoming law.

“The community embraced the Air Force for all those years, and then they moved out and left this mess — and they need to come back in and clean it up,” Peters told The Washington Sun.

The bill gives Peters the chance to shape a cleanup effort that will likely run for decades after his term ends in January. The military’s extensive use of firefighting foam containing PFAS — known as "forever chemicals" because they can persist in water, soil and air for decades — has potentially exposed service members, their families and nearby communities to health risks.

Peters, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, has worked on PFAS for much of his career. He successfully helped push the military to move away from its reliance on firefighting foam that contains these chemicals and provide alternative drinking water when community wells are contaminated by PFAS. A defense law signed last year included provisions he led requiring a Pentagon strategy to accelerate PFAS remediation and a public dashboard showing site-level progress and timelines.

But getting the Pentagon to address the contamination itself has required him and other lawmakers to keep up the pressure.

“I’ve been a dog on a bone when it comes to that,” he said.

The Pentagon has identified just under 600 current and former military installations that require further investigation and likely cleanup. Its latest public update delayed projected end dates for the investigation and feasibility-study stage for 243 installations.

Those dates are for the work of figuring out the extent of contamination and how to fix it. They are not deadlines for completing a permanent cleanup. Peters’ bill would push the Pentagon to take protective steps while that extended process continues, such as treating contaminated groundwater or removing heavily contaminated soil, depending on the site.

“We here in Grayling are very grateful for the support we have received from Senator Peters and are very concerned about the future support of the PFAS contamination in the state and our community,” said Ray Basile, the community co-chair for the Camp Grayling Restoration Advisory Board. A PFAS plume from the military base in Grayling, Michigan, is migrating toward the town’s water source. The community has been trying, without success, to push the Pentagon to invest in stopping it before it reaches the water supply.

A Government Accountability Office review described PFAS cleanup as an undertaking that could take decades and billions of dollars. Costs are expected to rise as investigators discover the contamination’s full extent and determine the remedies.

Peters argued the Pentagon already has the money to begin work, even if Congress ultimately needs to provide more.

“You have enough money to start,” he said. “Whether or not you have money to finish it may be different.”

The Pentagon declined to comment on the pending legislation, citing its policy of not doing so. It pointed to its public explanation that new water standards have required more sensitive testing and another look at previously evaluated sites.

It also said it is prioritizing sites with the highest health risks and that updated timelines don’t necessarily mean delayed cleanups. It said it is already taking interim steps, such as providing alternative drinking water, treating contaminated groundwater and removing contaminated soil.

John Conger, a former Pentagon official who oversaw environmental policy, said the legislation raised the question of whether the Defense Department and Environmental Protection Agency have enough staff to complete the necessary work.

“If you want to have 50 or 100 sites take action in a certain period of time, you need people to execute all of those things; you need people to work up the documents, you need people at the EPA to be able to sign off,” he said. “They have a limited capacity and a limited staff over there to handle all of this.”

Conger said the Defense Department could do more immediately to explain the delays to residents. When it changes a projected date, it should publish a reason alongside the new date. “It’s not complicated,” he said. “Then you’re giving people information so that they understand what the hell happened.”

Lawmakers have been urging the Pentagon under successive administrations to go faster. Under President Donald Trump, there have been three rounds of delays, some adding decades to the timetables.

Peters meanwhile has pursued a similar approach through the annual defense bill. A provision he secured in the Senate Armed Services Committee’s version would require interim action in at least 50 delayed sites.

MikeRounds (7017x4678, AR: 1.50)
Peters said he and the co-sponsor of Thursday’s measure, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), would work to expand the requirement in the defense bill to match their new standalone bill. Rounds’ home state has also faced lengthy delays: Investigation timelines at Ellsworth Air Force Base, Joe Foss Field Airport and Rapid City Regional Airport have slipped by at least a decade, according to the senators’ offices.

“I thought we had it on a schedule before, but we have new delays,” Rounds said. “The longer you delay, the more it disperses into the ground, which makes it more difficult and more expensive to clean up.”

If the expanded requirement does not become law before this Congress ends, lawmakers would have to pursue it again next year. Rounds said he intends to continue the work after Peters leaves, alongside other lawmakers from both parties.

“There are others that understand how serious it is, and this is something that impacts a lot of our Air Force bases,” he said. “Any place where you've had firefighting equipment over the years, there's PFAS in the groundwater or in and around the groundwater, and we just have to clean it up.”

Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who will become Michigan’s senior senator, said she intends to take a larger role in addressing PFAS contamination and protecting the Great Lakes. Pointing to her work on PFAS legislation in the House and turnover among several lawmakers involved in water issues, she called this “the right time for me to be stepping up.”

“This is one of a number of issues I plan on just taking on in the role of senior senator,” she said. “I’m excited to take the charge.”

Peters declined to designate a successor but pointed to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand’s (D-New York) involvement with the bill alongside Rounds and Slotkin. Asked whether he felt he had done enough, he said the scale and expense of the problem would require Congress’s attention for years to come.

“You can never do enough,” he said. “You have to keep working at it, and it's expensive to fix, so there's a lot of pushback. You just have to be persistent. You have to be dogged.”

The campaign for Peters’ seat — between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers — has not focused on Michigan’s PFAS issues, leaving the Grayling community uncertain about who will take up the mantle with Peters gone.

“We have yet to hear from either candidate about their position on this very important subject and the effects the PFAS contamination will continue to have on the health of our citizens,” Basile said.

Both candidates told The Sun the PFAS issue remains a priority should they win in November.

“This delay is another policy failure by an administration that, time and again, screws over Michigan, either through incompetence or malice. Bases in Michigan, like the former Wurtsmith Airforce Base, rely on cooperation from the federal government in order to keep our environment healthy and safe,” El-Sayed said. “Sen. Peters has led on this fight and … I want to carry that work forward.”

“Michigan families deserve to know their drinking water is safe and clean, and the firefighters who spend their careers protecting our communities deserve protection from further PFAS exposure,” Rogers said. “PFAS contamination ought to be cleaned up expeditiously.”

entries.title: Lawmakers Want Answers After F-35 Parts End Up in China
entries.summary: Senators from both parties have pressed for briefings: “Somebody really screwed up.”
entries.content:
Lawmakers are pressing the Trump administration for answers after F-35 components were diverted to Hong Kong, raising questions on Capitol Hill about how parts from the military’s most advanced fighter jet ended up in territory controlled by China.

The Pentagon and the F-35 Joint Program Office have said they are investigating the incident and working with U.S. authorities and industry partners. The parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — were being shipped via UPS from Australia to the United States for repair or disposal when they were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, according to Bloomberg.

The episode drew concern from senators in both parties Thursday, with several saying they want more information from the Pentagon about the circumstances of the shipment and whether China could gain anything of military value from the components.

Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the administration needs to explain and he expected to be briefed on the matter within several days.

“How did it happen? How did this take place?” Warner said. “It begs a lot of questions. Again, this administration's whole approach to national security in China is so episodic.”

Republicans, similarly, focused on how the components could have been diverted in the first place.

“I want to get briefed on it, but if that’s true, somebody really screwed up,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), a Senate Intelligence Committee member. “What a boneheaded thing to do.”

“But that certainly needs to be investigated. That's not the way things are supposed to work,” he added.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) said the incident could force Congress and the Pentagon to examine the logistics used to transport military equipment, including the government’s reliance on private shippers.

Cramer, who chairs the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on Airland, said he was focused for now on what China might learn from the particular components rather than how they came to be in China’s possession.

“We don’t know whether it was an aggressive move by the Chinese, whether it was a preplanned thing, whether it was simply an accident,” he said. “

Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles has said the components were not sensitive, while acknowledging they ended up in Hong Kong. The Lockheed Martin-made F-35 incorporates classified technologies that include stealth coatings and advanced radar and sensors.

“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred,” Marles said this week.

Members of the Senate Armed Services Committee said they wanted the Pentagon to determine what went wrong. Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) said she expects the Pentagon to investigate the issue and brief Congress when “they have something.”

“I’m sure it’s being investigated by the department right now, and yeah, we’ll ask for updates during that,” Fischer said.

The questions over the F-35 shipment arose as Chinese President Xi Jinping was in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump, putting the incident alongside a broader debate about how the U.S. should manage its relationship with Beijing.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) — who this week criticized the lavish reception the president offered Xi and urged Trump to press the “brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator” on security and human rights — offered a terse assessment of the F-35 situation: “It’s troubling.”

Several senators argued that diplomatic engagement remained necessary even as they described Beijing as a military and economic rival. Cramer said maintaining a relationship was better than having none at all, despite calling China America’s “No. 1 adversary.”

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida) took a harder line and suggested that while Trump is rolling out the red carpet in public, he has to press Xi in private, particularly on imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai. Still, Scott conceded Trump must be diplomatic given China’s chokehold on critical minerals — which the U.S. relies on for weapons, electric vehicles and more.

“China is not going to be our friend,” Scott said.

entries.title: Senate Votes Down a Resolution to End the War with Iran
entries.summary: Many senators backed the president’s war powers despite frustration from voters.
entries.content:
Most Senate Republicans and Democratic Sen. John Fetterman voted down a resolution meant to curb President Donald Trump’s war powers, even as frustration with the nearly seven-month war spills into the midterm campaign.

The resolution, which the House approved in July, failed in a 49-50 vote. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis, Rand Paul, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joined nearly all Democrats in support.

The resolution is largely symbolic. But this vote came at a more precarious moment for Trump, with Republicans facing growing anger over the conflict’s duration, rising fuel prices and the administration’s failure to explain how it plans to end the fighting.

Tillis (R-North Carolina) supported an Iran war powers resolution for the first time after opposing previous efforts to restrain Trump.

Tillis said Wednesday that the vote was important to get “some strategic clarity around here so we can measure our success.”

The senator, who is not seeking reelection, warned in July that he would take a “very different posture” if the fighting continued beyond Sept. 10, 60 days after the administration formally notified Congress that hostilities had resumed and restarted the war powers clock, an interpretation lawmakers in both parties have questioned.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), who is also retiring after this year, remained opposed to the resolution despite hearing criticism of the war from his constituents. He declined to explain his vote on Thursday.

Last week, the House passed a separate war powers resolution 220-204. Every Democrat voted in favor of the House resolution, along with seven Republicans — four more than had backed previous efforts to check Trump’s war powers. Reps. Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn supported an Iran war powers resolution for the first time last week.

Miller-Meeks and Nunn represent competitive Iowa districts where voters have faced rising diesel, gasoline and fertilizer prices.

The resolution directs Trump to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress declares war or specifically authorizes military action. It allows forces needed to defend the U.S. or an ally or partner from an imminent attack to remain.

Democrats have used war powers votes to put lawmakers on the record and register their opposition to the war. The White House argues that Congress cannot force the president to end the campaign this way and that Trump has sufficient authority under Article 2 of the Constitution.

Republican criticism of the war has moved beyond lawmakers who have consistently challenged Trump on constitutional grounds.

Republican Senate candidates Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Mike Rogers of Michigan called this week for the war to end quickly as rising fuel prices squeeze voters. Hinson had voted against six House efforts to restrain Trump.

Recent polls show growing opposition to the war. A CNN/SSRS survey found that just 26% approve of Trump’s handling of the conflict, while 78% say he is not doing enough to end it. His approval among Republicans has fallen from 73% in March to 60%. A Marquette poll found that 79% of Americans say the war has not been worth the cost.

The Pentagon’s public database lists 19 American service members killed and more than 820 wounded. U.S. Central Command estimated that the fighting cost $43.6 billion through Sept. 3.

entries.title: The Wizards Expect Alex Sarr to Be Ready for Opening Night
entries.summary: Plus more notes from GM Will Dawkins’ Thursday news conference, including a “motivated” Anthony Davis.
entries.content:
The Wizards expect to have Alex Sarr available on opening night against the Milwaukee Bucks, as the former No. 2 overall pick is recovering from having fractured his right foot in an offseason workout in June.

General manager Will Dawkins said Thursday in his annual preseason news conference that Sarr will be a “partial participant” in training camp, but should be healthy by Oct. 21 when the team opens the season at home. Sarr improved in his second year of the NBA, averaging 16.3 points and 7.4 rebounds per game.

The injury news isn’t as good for Jamir Watkins, who tore his ACL in the team’s summer league opener. Dawkins said that Watkins is still recovering, and there’s no timetable for his return. Watkins was one of the Wizards’ best perimeter defenders as a rookie and was expected to compete for minutes this season before getting hurt.

“He’ll be out a good amount of time,” Dawkins said of Watkins.

Here are more takeaways from Dawkins’ session with reporters:

Anthony Davis is “motivated.”

Dawkins declined to discuss Davis’ contract situation, after both sides decided to postpone extension talks over the summer and wait until after a quarter of the regular season has gone by before resuming. Davis will make $58 million this season and has a $62 million player option for next season.

Since August, he’s been eligible for a four-year, $275 million extension that averages nearly $69 million per year. But Davis, 33, has played in just 71 games combined the past two seasons due to injuries. He didn’t play for the Wizards at all last season after being traded by the Mavericks in February because of an injured hand.

“[Davis] is in a great frame of mind,” Dawkins said. “He’s focused and ready to start the season. He’s very much a motivated player right now. And I expect AD to remind the basketball world who he really is.”
Will Dawkins Trae Young (7334x4890, AR: 1.50)Dawkins is bullish on Trae Young.

Young hasn’t played much more than Davis and appeared in just five games for the Wizards last season after being traded by the Hawks. Despite that brief tenure, Dawkins gave Young a four-year, $212.8 million contract that raised some eyebrows across the NBA.

“Bringing back Trae Young was very, very important to us,” Dawkins said.

Dawkins said Young “really liked the young talent around him” and expects his starting point guard to embrace the challenge.

“I think he’s read a lot of things that were said about him,” Dawkins said. “He probably didn’t like how last season went in terms of injury and health, and he’s here to prove that he’s healthy and he hasn’t changed who he is as a player and can have an impact in making others better at a high level.”

The Wizards expect AJ Dybantsa to help right away.

The 19-year-old No. 1 overall draft pick steps into a unique situation where he isn’t expected to be the focal point of the team right away, given the presence of Young, Davis and Washington’s other young contributors.

Dawkins said Dybantsa’s work ethic has impressed him so far, but tempered expectations for how much the 6-foot-9 forward is going to impact winning as a rookie.

“He’s definitely going to help us now,” Dawkins said. “But more so in the future.”

On the whole, Dawkins, who is entering his fourth season running the front office, told reporters that the team believes it “is starting to construct something that is going to be sustainable” and is expecting to “increase the moments of competitive basketball we play in.”

entries.title: Mark Carney Says He Has Prepared for the Possibility of a U.S. Invasion
entries.summary: “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to,” the Canadian prime minister told The New York Times.
entries.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said during a lengthy interview this week that he has prepared for the possibility, however unlikely, of a U.S. incursion onto Canadian soil.

The stunning remarks come as President Donald Trump has increased his provocations of America’s northern neighbor and embarked on a bitter trade war that has prompted a strong response from Carney.

Trump has repeatedly called for Canada to become the 51st state, including posting pictures on social media that depict Canada as part of the United States or sharing a map of North America draped in the U.S. flag. The president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” last month.

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney, who has emerged as one of the world’s most prominent voices challenging Trump, told The New York Times during an interview on Wednesday. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to.”

While Carney, a former banker and economist, did not detail what considerations had been taken into account, he said that Canada and the U.S. maintain an open line of communication.

“We have a good relationship in the sense of we can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” Carney said. “That exists and that will continue to exist.”

The U.S. entered a tit-for-tat trade war with Canada after economic talks between the two countries collapsed this summer. A new round of steep tariffs — which reached 50% for certain products in late August — has been unpopular among both Republicans in the U.S. and Canadian residents, many of whom recently signed a petition to oust U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

Carney told the Times he has planned to diversify Canada’s suppliers in an effort to reduce the country’s reliance on the U.S. for certain products, including technology.

Still, the prime minister said a “mutually beneficial” deal between the countries is on the table. He pointed to Canada’s oil exports to the U.S., as well as the fertilizer ingredient potash. Trump said earlier this week that he wants to start trading with Belarus — which already faces U.S. sanctions over its ties to Russia and would involve more complicated shipping logistics — instead of continuing to import almost 90% of its stores from Canada, which has the world’s largest reserve.

“I think this is a doable component of the deal, and there are other examples that exist, and we’re ready to work toward,” Carney said of Canada’s potash supply.

entries.title: Maryland Residents Voice Concerns Over Proposal to Build $1.4B Sphere
entries.summary: A public hearing on the project drew a large group of union members advocating for a labor agreement for workers.
entries.content:
The Sphere in Las Vegas may have a Maryland relative by 2030 if the Prince George’s County Council approves a $1.4 billion proposal to build the entertainment venue, but local workers want to secure a labor agreement first.

During a public meeting in Largo on Tuesday, council members fielded residents’ concerns over Sphere Entertainment’s plans to construct the 6,000-seat venue, which would have about a third of the capacity of the Las Vegas space, on a 15-acre lot just north of MGM National Harbor.

At the start of the meeting, Paul Macchia, senior vice president of government affairs and social impact for Sphere Entertainment, said the Sphere would generate an estimated $1.3 billion in economic activity to the county and $1.5 billion across the state, based on projections from the Las Vegas Sphere’s performance.

“We think National Harbor is the perfect location for a world-class venue like Sphere,” Macchia said. “In every community where we operate, we strive to be good neighbors.”

The packed crowd was mostly composed of union members who called for a project labor agreement and want a say in employment terms to ensure a fair deal for workers.

Sphere Entertainment’s presentation expressed a “commitment to organized labor” and stated the project would generate more than 12,000 new jobs for construction and supporting businesses and services, with 3,300 of those construction jobs in Prince George’s County.

The presentation also stated that more than 97% of the tradespeople employed during construction of the Las Vegas Sphere were union workers, and 45% of its current staff are union-represented.

“All the companies in the Madison Square Garden family of companies, including Sphere Entertainment, are exceptionally union-friendly,” Macchia said. “We have excellent relations with labor unions in Vegas, New York and Chicago, and we fully expect those relations to continue here in Prince George’s County.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Lamar Mutts of the Eastern Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters, who asked his fellow union members to stand before his public comment, said he wasn’t sure local workers have a “seat at the table” regarding a labor agreement.

“Sphere has talked about its strong relationship with unions on its Vegas and New York projects, but when asked about a project labor agreement here in Prince George’s County, we’re told ‘There’s nothing to talk about at this time,’” Mutts said. “That concerns me.”

Prince George’s County Council Chair Krystal Oriadha told WTOP that any public financing must guarantee protected jobs and minority business hiring and that the county is exploring whether the project could help fund a rail connection.

Oriadha and other council members have pressed the Sphere to adopt a project labor agreement, according to The Baltimore Banner. In a meeting of the council's planning, housing and development committee the day before the listening session, Oriadha told a Sphere executive, "There will [be] inclusion of labor. Period," the Banner reported.

The proposal still faces committee reviews and a public hearing ahead of an October vote, she said.

If approved, site work for the project would begin in early 2027, according to Sphere Entertainment’s presentation.

entries.title: Final RFK Campus and Commanders Stadium Plan Heads to D.C. Council
entries.summary: The $3.8 billion riverfront project moves closer to reality as officials eye construction starting in the spring.
entries.content:
Mayor Muriel Bowser submitted the finalized “master plan” for the RFK Stadium Campus to the D.C. Council on Thursday, laying out a roadmap to transform 180 acres of largely dormant riverfront property into a bustling, multi-use community centered around the Washington Commanders’ future home.

Anchored by a stadium with a nearly $3.8 billion price tag — $1.1 billion in public funding for site preparation and parking decks, plus $2.7 billion from the team — the 186-page plan is hailed by project leaders as a generational opportunity to build a campus with enough amenities to attract visitors even when the stadium is not hosting an event.

Once realized, Bowser said, the plan will deliver a “whole new neighborhood” to Ward 7.

“As our economy shifts and we have less federal activity, we have to have more of everything else, and that includes hospitality, sports and economic development,” Bowser said at a news conference Thursday.

Officials say the final version came after months of localized outreach and more than 3,000 public comments submitted following the release of a draft plan in June. Revisions in the final documents include plans for a new transit plaza, guidance to build retail parking underground and the formal inclusion of the D.C. Armory into the master plan’s boundaries to evaluate its future redevelopment.

Ward 7 council member Wendell Felder said the council will hold a hearing on the master plan Wednesday, with lawmakers expected to vote on officially adopting the blueprint before the end of the year. He said his office will host a site walkthrough for residents later that day, emphasizing that “this cannot simply be a plan that is developed for our community without our community.”

Brian Hanlon, director of D.C.’s Department of Buildings who is also heading the RFK project management office, said the city expects to hit the ground running: Bidding for construction will begin in November and December, with stadium foundation work slated for the spring. It’s expected to open in 2030.

The planned 65,000-seat stadium has been presented as a modernized upgrade designed to host roughly 200 events per year. Interior renderings that the Commanders recently released showcase a single-tier seating bowl designed to eliminate obstructed views, and a steep, end-zone “fan wall” modeled after NBA arenas to maximize crowd noise.

The stadium is just one piece of a development footprint that officials say will generate some $4 billion in tax revenue and create 30,000 construction jobs as well as 2,000 permanent positions. While there is no official timeline for the surrounding campus to be completed, officials say it will contain between 5,500 and 6,500 new homes — with at least 30 percent designated as affordable — alongside commercial spaces, a grocery store and other promised amenities.

The plan mandates that 30 percent of the site be preserved as publicly accessible parks and green space, including a new indoor-outdoor recreation complex. It also promises to drastically expand access to the Anacostia River. Bowser likened that potential riverfront transformation to the development of The Wharf, a massive, multibillion-dollar dining and residential destination that revitalized the city’s Southwest waterfront.

Still, how fans will actually get to and from the stadium remains a contentious hurdle. While city officials expect a significant number of fans to use public transit, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority General Manager Randy Clarke and the outgoing mayor have ruled out building a new Metrorail station. A summary document from the city's Office of Planning notes that WMATA concluded the idea was infeasible due to “cost, engineering and timeline constraints.”

Instead, Metro plans to expand the mezzanine and entrance at the existing Stadium-Armory station and launch a rapid bus route called the Gold Line that would run along H Street and Benning Road Northeast. This strategy has disappointed some local residents and officials who argue that an entirely new Metro station is key to supporting long-term neighborhood growth.

Asked what happens if the Gold Line isn’t funded or ready by opening day, Bowser stood firm.

“It will be,” she said, adding that funding streetscape and transit enhancements in the surrounding neighborhoods will strengthen residents’ connections to business and job opportunities. “This is our obligation.”
